m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain the difference between a Raspberry Pi Pico W and a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, and what each does in an IoT system.
  • Open a MicroPython project for the Pico W in Wokwi and find main.py, diagram.json, the play button, and the Serial Monitor.
  • Read the Pico W's pinout: GP numbers, physical pin numbers, the analog pins, and the power pins.
  • Install Thonny or Raspberry Pi Imager if you own real hardware, and fix the setup problems people hit most.

The name "Raspberry Pi" covers two very different machines. A Raspberry Pi 5 is a full computer: it boots Linux, runs a desktop and a web browser, and has gigabytes of memory. A Raspberry Pi Pico W is a microcontroller board the size of a stick of gum with 264 KB of RAM. It has no operating system and runs exactly one program, but that program is running a fraction of a second after you plug the board in, and it can read a sensor and send the value over Wi-Fi.

Real IoT systems use both kinds. Small, cheap, low-power boards sit next to the plants or the door, and a bigger computer collects their data and shows a dashboard. This course builds that system, and you can do all of it in a browser for free.

#Two boards, two jobs

Raspberry Pi Pico W Raspberry Pi 4 or 5
What it is A microcontroller board (RP2040 chip plus a Wi-Fi chip) A single-board Linux computer
What runs on it One MicroPython program, started from main.py at power-up Raspberry Pi OS, with many programs at once
Its job in this course The sensor node: read sensors, drive LEDs and servos, send readings Optional: the Linux machine for the terminal lessons, an MQTT broker, or a dashboard
Cost to follow along $0 in Wokwi $0 (every lesson has a simulated or browser path)

You need a computer with a recent version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari and an internet connection. Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, and Linux all work. You don't need an account to run simulations; a free Wokwi account only matters for saving projects, which lesson 3 covers.

#Open your first Pico W project in Wokwi

  1. Go to wokwi.com and click the Pi Pico tile under Simulate with Wokwi Online.
  2. Under Starter Templates, find the Pi Pico W row and click Micropython Pico W. (The direct address is wokwi.com/projects/new/micropython-pi-pico-w. Bookmark it.)
  3. Be careful to pick the MicroPython template. The plain Pi Pico W tile starts an Arduino C++ project, and the Pico 2W tiles use a newer chip.

The project opens with code on the left and a drawing of the board on the right. The template's main.py contains three lines:

Press the green play button. After a moment, Hello, Pi Pico W! appears in a terminal panel under the board. That panel is the Serial Monitor: everything your program prints shows up there, and it's also where you type to the board. The short sleep exists because the board talks to the terminal over a simulated USB connection, and text printed before that connection is ready is lost.

#What each part of the editor does

  • main.py is your program. MicroPython runs it automatically every time the board starts, exactly like a real Pico W does at power-up.
  • diagram.json describes every part and wire in the circuit as text. Dragging parts around rewrites it, and pasting a whole circuit into it is the fastest way to build the lessons' circuits.
  • Library Manager adds libraries. You won't need it in the early modules.
  • Extra tabs are extra files. Wokwi copies every file in the project onto the board's simulated flash drive, so a second file such as sensors.py can be imported from main.py.
  • The blue + button above the diagram adds parts (or press A with the diagram selected). To draw a wire, click one pin, then another.
  • The green play button starts the board; while it runs, the same spot stops it.

#Read the Pico W's pinout

Zoom in on the board (scroll, or press +) and hover over a pin to see its name. The pins have two kinds of numbers, and mixing them up is the most common wiring mistake in this course. Physical pin numbers count around the board: pin 1 is at the top left next to the USB connector, pins 1 to 20 run down the left edge, and 21 to 40 run up the right edge. GP numbers are what your code uses. Pin(15) means GP15, which sits at physical pin 20.

Physical pins Name What it is for
1, 2, 4–7, 9–12, 14–17, 19–22, 24–27, 29 GP0 to GP22 Digital input and output; any of them can do PWM
31, 32, 34 GP26, GP27, GP28 Digital pins that can also measure voltage (analog inputs ADC0 to ADC2)
3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28, 38 GND Ground, the 0 V reference every circuit returns to
33 AGND A quieter ground for analog sensors
36 3V3(OUT) 3.3 V for powering small sensors
39 and 40 VSYS and VBUS Power input, and the 5 V that arrives from USB
30, 35, 37 RUN, ADC_VREF, 3V3_EN Special pins; leave them unconnected

The Pico W's onboard LED is a special case. On the original Pico it was wired to GP25, but on the Pico W it hangs off the Wi-Fi chip, so MicroPython reaches it by name: Pin("LED").

⚠️ Watch out

Every GPIO pin on the Pico W is a 3.3 V pin. VBUS carries 5 V when USB is plugged in, and connecting it to any GP pin can destroy the chip. The simulator won't warn you, so build the habit now: power sensors from 3V3(OUT), not VBUS. Module 2 explains why.

#Optional: set up a real Pico W or Raspberry Pi

Skip this section if you're staying in the simulator; nothing later depends on it. If you have hardware, pick your computer below. Thonny is a free Python editor that talks to a Pico W over USB. Raspberry Pi Imager writes Raspberry Pi OS onto a microSD card for a Pi 4 or 5.

Windows

  • Thonny: download the Windows installer from thonny.org, run it, and accept the defaults.
  • Imager: download Raspberry Pi Imager for Windows from raspberrypi.com/software and run the installer.
  • SSH, for lesson 2: Windows 10 and 11 include the ssh command. Open PowerShell from the Start menu to use it.

macOS

  • Thonny: download the macOS package from thonny.org, open it, and follow the installer.
  • Imager: download Raspberry Pi Imager for macOS from raspberrypi.com/software, open the file, and drag the app into Applications.
  • SSH, for lesson 2: open Terminal (in Applications › Utilities). The ssh command is built in.

Chromebook

  • Thonny: turn on the Linux development environment in Settings › About ChromeOS › Developers, open the Terminal app, and run sudo apt install thonny. When you plug in a Pico W, ChromeOS asks whether to connect it to Linux; say yes.
  • Imager: Raspberry Pi Imager doesn't run on ChromeOS. Borrow a Windows, macOS, or Linux computer for the ten minutes it takes to write the card, or use a kit whose card comes with Raspberry Pi OS already on it.
  • SSH, for lesson 2: use the Linux Terminal app. If ssh says command not found, run sudo apt install openssh-client.

Linux

  • Thonny: on Debian, Ubuntu, or Raspberry Pi OS, run sudo apt install thonny (Raspberry Pi OS with desktop already has it).
  • Imager: on Ubuntu, sudo apt install rpi-imager, or download the AppImage from raspberrypi.com/software.
  • SSH, for lesson 2: the ssh command is almost always installed; if not, sudo apt install openssh-client.

Put MicroPython on a real Pico W. Hold down the white BOOTSEL button and plug the board into your computer with a micro-USB cable, then let go. A drive called RPI-RP2 appears. Download the Pico W .uf2 file from micropython.org/download/RPI_PICO_W and drag it onto that drive; the board reboots into MicroPython. (Thonny can do the same step for you from Tools › Options › Interpreter: choose MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico), then use its link for installing or updating MicroPython.) Afterwards, select the same interpreter in Thonny and you get a >>> prompt from the board.

Prepare a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5. Insert a microSD card into your computer and open Imager. Pick your model on the Device tab, Raspberry Pi OS on the OS tab, and your card on the Storage tab. Keep Exclude system drives turned on so you can't erase your own computer. On the Customisation tabs, set a hostname (this course uses iotpi), your time zone, a username and password, and your Wi-Fi, and on Remote Access turn on Enable SSH with password authentication. Review the summary, select Write, and wait for it to finish verifying.

#Fixes for the problems people actually hit

  • Wokwi never loads, or the play button spins forever. School networks sometimes block simulator sites. Try another network or browser, and close extra tabs on an older laptop. The first run of a session can take several seconds while the firmware loads.
  • The terminal stays empty. Check you picked the MicroPython template, since an Arduino project shows different text. If you deleted the time.sleep(0.1) line, put it back so early prints aren't lost.
  • Keyboard shortcuts such as A or R do nothing. Click an empty spot on the diagram first. In Firefox, turn off the setting Search for text when you start typing, which steals those keys.
  • (Real Pico W) No RPI-RP2 drive appears. Many micro-USB cables carry power only. Try another cable, and make sure you hold BOOTSEL before plugging in.
  • (Real Pico W) Thonny says it can't find the device. Click the interpreter name in the bottom-right corner of Thonny and pick MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico) with the right port. Close any other program that might be holding the port.
  • (Raspberry Pi) Imager can't see the card. Try another USB card reader. Built-in readers on some laptops are unreliable.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your code says Pin(15). Which physical pin should the wire go to?

  • Physical pin 15 is GP11. Code always uses GP numbers, not positions.

  • Pin(15) means GP15, which sits at physical pin 20 at the bottom of the left edge.

  • The simulator only connects the pins you wire. A wire on the wrong pin does nothing.

Show answer

B. Pin(15) means GP15, which sits at physical pin 20 at the bottom of the left edge.

2A light sensor needs power. Which pin should feed it?

  • VBUS is 5 V from USB. A sensor powered at 5 V can send 5 V back into a 3.3 V GPIO pin and damage it.

  • It provides 3.3 V, the same level the GPIO pins use, so the sensor's output can't exceed what the pins accept.

  • GP28 is a signal pin. It's meant to read the sensor's output, not to power it.

Show answer

B. It provides 3.3 V, the same level the GPIO pins use, so the sensor's output can't exceed what the pins accept.

3Which job fits a Pico W better than a Raspberry Pi 5?

  • It starts in a fraction of a second, runs one program, and costs a few dollars, which is ideal for a sensor node.

  • That needs an operating system and much more memory; it's a job for a Linux computer.

  • The Pico W has no desktop. You edit on another computer (or in Wokwi) and the board runs the result.

Show answer

A. It starts in a fraction of a second, runs one program, and costs a few dollars, which is ideal for a sensor node.

Key takeaways

  • A Pico W is a microcontroller that runs one MicroPython program; a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 is a Linux computer. IoT systems often use both.
  • In Wokwi, choose Pi Pico › Micropython Pico W. main.py runs at start-up, diagram.json holds the circuit, and prints appear in the Serial Monitor.
  • Code uses GP numbers; wires go to physical pins. GP26 to GP28 can read analog voltages.
  • GPIO pins are 3.3 V only. Power sensors from 3V3(OUT), never from VBUS.

#Further reading

  • Wokwi's MicroPython guide (opens in a new tab): how Wokwi copies your files to the board and how to reach the REPL.
  • MicroPython quick reference for the RP2 (opens in a new tab): one page of working snippets for pins, PWM, ADC, Wi-Fi, and timers, kept up to date with the firmware.
  • Raspberry Pi Pico W datasheet (opens in a new tab): the official pinout drawing and what each power pin can supply.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a MicroPython program in Wokwi and read its output in the Serial Monitor.
  • Blink the onboard LED with Pin("LED") and an external LED on GP15.
  • Paste a circuit into diagram.json and check the LED is wired the right way round.
  • Stop a running program with Ctrl+C and control pins by hand from the REPL.
  • (Optional) Log in to a Raspberry Pi with SSH and blink an LED with gpiozero.

Blinking an LED is the "hello, world" of hardware, and it earns that place. If the light flashes, you have proved that your editor, the firmware, your code, and your wiring all work together. When something breaks later, a quick blink test tells you which of those four is at fault.

By the end of this lesson, two LEDs take turns: the tiny one on the board and a green one you wired yourself. The Serial Monitor counts the blinks.

#Step 1: Run the template

Open a new Micropython Pico W project (wokwi.com/projects/new/micropython-pi-pico-w) and press play. Hello, Pi Pico W! appears in the Serial Monitor.

Now press stop. Every run starts the board fresh, like unplugging a real one and plugging it back in. Variables don't survive between runs, which matters once you start logging data in Module 4.

#Step 2: Blink the onboard LED

Replace everything in main.py with this and press play:

The small LED near the USB connector flashes twice a second. Three lines do the work:

  • Pin("LED", Pin.OUT) creates an object for the onboard LED and makes it an output, a pin your code drives on or off. On the Pico W the LED is wired to the Wi-Fi chip rather than an ordinary GP pin, which is why it's named instead of numbered.
  • led.toggle() flips it: on becomes off, off becomes on.
  • time.sleep(0.25) pauses for a quarter second. On, wait, off, wait: one full blink every half second.

The while True: loop never ends, and that's normal for a microcontroller. There's no operating system to return to, so the program's job is to run until the power goes.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change 0.25 to 0.05 and run it again. Then try 2. Notice that while the board is sleeping it does nothing else at all; Module 3 shows how to blink without freezing the rest of the program.

#Step 3: Add an LED and a resistor

An LED on its own would pull as much current as the pin can push, which overheats both. A resistor in series limits the current. With 3.3 V from the pin, about 2 V dropped across a green LED, and 330 Ω, the current is (3.3 − 2.0) / 330 ≈ 4 mA: bright enough to see and gentle on the pin. Module 2 works through this math properly.

You can wire it with the mouse (blue + button, then click pin to pin), but pasting is faster and exact. Open the diagram.json tab, select everything, and replace it with:

Each connection lists two pins as part:pin. pico:GND.4 is the fourth ground pin, physical pin 18, just above GP14 and GP15. led1:A is the LED's anode, its positive leg, and led1:C is the cathode. Current only flows from anode to cathode, so an LED wired backwards stays dark without any error message. The env line tells Wokwi which MicroPython firmware to load; it's the same value the template uses.

Drag the parts anywhere you like. The wires follow.

#Step 4: Make the two LEDs take turns

Replace main.py with the finished program:

The two LEDs alternate, and every five seconds the Serial Monitor gets a new line:

value(1) and value(0) set a pin high (3.3 V) or low (0 V) directly, which is clearer than toggle() when two pins must stay opposite. The blinks % 10 == 0 check prints only every tenth blink, so the terminal doesn't scroll by too fast to read.

⚠️ Watch out

The external LED never lights. Check three things in this order: the pin number in code matches the wire (Pin(15) needs pico:GP15), the LED's anode faces the resistor and its cathode faces GND, and the wire really ends on a pin. In Wokwi, hovering over a wire end shows which pin it reached.

#Step 5: Take over from the REPL

Click inside the Serial Monitor and press Ctrl+C. The program stops with a KeyboardInterrupt message and you land at the MicroPython prompt, >>>, called the REPL (read, evaluate, print, loop). The variables from main.py are still there, so you can drive the pins by hand:

The first line lights the green LED and leaves it on. sys.platform reports 'rp2', the name of MicroPython's port for Raspberry Pi's microcontroller chips. The REPL is the fastest way to test one line of code or check how a sensor responds before writing a whole program around it.

#Step 6 (optional): Blink an LED on a real Raspberry Pi over SSH

If you prepared a Raspberry Pi with Imager in lesson 1 (hostname iotpi, SSH turned on), you can control its GPIO pins from your own computer's terminal. With the Pi powered off, wire GPIO17 (physical pin 11) through a 330 Ω resistor to the LED's long leg, and the short leg to GND (physical pin 9). Then power it up, wait a minute for the first boot, and connect, replacing student with the username you chose:

The first time, SSH asks you to trust the Pi:

Type yes, then your password (nothing appears while you type it; that's deliberate). The prompt changes to student@iotpi:~ $, and every command you type now runs on the Pi. Make a folder and a file:

In the nano editor, type this program, then save with Ctrl+O and Enter and exit with Ctrl+X:

Run it with python3 blink.py and stop it with Ctrl+C. Notice the difference from MicroPython: gpiozero's blink() runs in the background, so the program needs pause() to stay alive. Type exit to end the SSH session.

  • Could not resolve hostname iotpi.local: the Pi may still be booting, or your network doesn't pass .local names. Find the Pi's IP address in your router's device list and use ssh student@192.168.1.57 (with its real address) instead.
  • Permission denied, please try again.: the username or password doesn't match what you set in Imager. Usernames are lowercase.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the Pico W code use Pin("LED") instead of Pin(25)?

  • Speed has nothing to do with it; both would switch in microseconds.

  • On the original Pico it was GP25, but on the Pico W MicroPython reaches it through the wireless chip by name.

  • Regular pins use numbers, like Pin(15). Only special pins such as the LED have names.

Show answer

B. On the original Pico it was GP25, but on the Pico W MicroPython reaches it through the wireless chip by name.

2You swap the LED's two legs in diagram.json. What happens when you run the program?

  • The code has no idea how the LED is wired; it only sets the pin high or low.

  • An LED is a diode: current flows only from anode to cathode, so a reversed LED doesn't light at all.

  • That silence is why "check the LED's direction" is on every hardware debugging checklist.

Show answer

C. That silence is why "check the LED's direction" is on every hardware debugging checklist.

3Your program runs a while True: loop. How do you get to the >>> prompt without restarting the simulation?

  • That raises KeyboardInterrupt, stops main.py, and leaves its variables available at the prompt.

  • Stop ends the whole simulation, so there's no board left to type to.

  • while True: never finishes on its own.

Show answer

A. That raises KeyboardInterrupt, stops main.py, and leaves its variables available at the prompt.

Key takeaways

  • Pin(id, Pin.OUT) makes an output; value(1) sets it to 3.3 V, value(0) to 0 V, and toggle() flips it.
  • The Pico W's onboard LED is Pin("LED"); external LEDs use GP numbers and need a series resistor.
  • Wokwi circuits live in diagram.json as parts plus part:pin connections. A reversed LED fails silently.
  • Ctrl+C in the Serial Monitor stops main.py and opens the REPL, where you can test single lines.
  • On a Raspberry Pi, ssh user@host.local gives you its terminal, and gpiozero's LED(17) drives GPIO17.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Make the external LED blink out SOS in Morse code: three short, three long, three short.
  • Add a second external LED on GP14 and make the three LEDs chase each other.
  • Print the time since start-up with each count, using time.ticks_ms().

#Further reading

  • MicroPython's machine.Pin reference (opens in a new tab): every way to configure a pin, including pull-ups, which Module 3 uses.
  • Wokwi's diagram.json format (opens in a new tab): what each field means and how to shape wires with the placement mini-language.
  • gpiozero recipes (opens in a new tab): short, tested programs for LEDs, buttons, and sensors on a Raspberry Pi.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Save Wokwi projects with an account, as a ZIP, or as plain files, and know who can see a saved project.
  • Read a MicroPython traceback and fix the four errors beginners see most.
  • Follow a fixed order of checks when a circuit doesn't work.
  • Keep secrets out of simulator projects, use Wokwi from the keyboard, and handle real hardware safely.

Here's a message you will see this week:

It looks like a wall, but it answers three questions in order: which file (main.py), which line (6), and what went wrong (a name that doesn't exist yet). Read the last line first, then jump to the line number. Most errors in this course take less than a minute to fix once you read them that way.

#Save your work, and know who can see it

A Wokwi project lives in your browser tab until you save it. You have three options:

  1. A free Wokwi account. Sign in, then click Save. The project gets its own web address, and Share gives you a link to send. Free projects are public: anyone with the link can open them, and they can appear in Wokwi's lists of recent projects. Keeping projects unlisted is a paid feature.
  2. Download a ZIP. The project menu next to Save includes Download project ZIP, which saves main.py, diagram.json, and any other files to your computer.
  3. Copy the files by hand. Select all the text in each tab and paste it into a file with the same name on your computer. It always works, even when you can't sign in.

Whichever you use, keep one folder per project on your own computer. A layout like this makes it easy to find last week's circuit when a later module builds on it:

#The four errors you'll see most

MicroPython's messages are shorter than regular Python's, but they mean the same things.

Last line of the traceback What it means Usual fix
NameError: name 'led' isn't defined You used a name before creating it, or spelled it differently (LED and led are different names) Check the spelling and that the line creating it runs first
AttributeError: 'Pin' object has no attribute 'vlaue' The object exists, but it has no method with that name Fix the typo (value) or look up the method in the docs
ImportError: no module named 'umqtt' That library isn't on the board Check the spelling; if it's right, the library has to be added to the project as a file
OSError: [Errno 2] ENOENT A file you tried to open doesn't exist on the board's flash Create it first, or check the file name and folder

One more is worth knowing by sight: IndentationError: unexpected indent. MicroPython is as strict about indentation as regular Python, and pasting code from a web page sometimes adds a space at the start of a line.

💡 Tip

When an error mentions a line number, look at the line just above it too. A missing closing bracket on line 5 is often reported on line 6.

#A debugging routine for hardware

When nothing happens, the fault could be in the code, the wiring, or the part. Guessing wastes time. Check in this order, because each step is quicker than the next and rules out a whole category:

The second question is the one people skip. Adding print("about to turn on LED") just before the line that should do something tells you instantly whether the problem is before that line or after it. Leave the prints in while you work, and remove them once it does.

#Keep secrets out of the simulator

Two facts about Wokwi's free plan shape how this course handles passwords:

  • Free projects are public. Anything in main.py can be read by anyone who finds the link.
  • Wokwi's public internet gateway is monitored. When the simulated Pico W goes online, its traffic passes through Wokwi's servers, and Wokwi's documentation says plainly not to send private or sensitive data through it.

So the simulated board joins Wokwi-GUEST, an open network with no password, and the course never asks you to type a real password, API key, or home address into a Wokwi project. Use made-up device names like greenhouse-01, not your name or school. Module 7 shows how real devices keep credentials out of their source code.

#Use Wokwi from the keyboard

You can build and run every circuit without precise mouse work:

  • With the diagram selected, A adds a part, R rotates the selected part, the arrow keys move it, D duplicates it, and Delete removes it. + and − zoom, and F fits the whole circuit in view.
  • A potentiometer responds to the keyboard while the simulation runs: click it, then use Left and Right for small steps, Page Up and Page Down for big ones, and Home or End for the ends of its range.
  • A pushbutton can have a keyboard key. Add "key": "b" to its attrs in diagram.json, and holding B holds the button down.
  • Browser zoom (Ctrl and +, or ⌘ and + on a Mac) enlarges the code and the Serial Monitor text. Every chart in these lessons has a text description, and the videos have captions in their YouTube settings.

#Work safely with real parts

The simulator can't be damaged. Real boards can, and so can fingers if something overheats. If you build on a desk:

  • Unplug before you rewire. Moving wires on a powered board is how pins end up briefly connected to the wrong thing.
  • 3.3 V only on GPIO pins. Never connect 5 V, VBUS, or a 5 V sensor's output directly to a Pico W or Raspberry Pi GPIO pin.
  • Every LED gets a resistor, and nothing connects 3V3 straight to GND. That's a short circuit.
  • Motors never run from a GPIO pin. Even small motors need a driver board and their own power supply. A micro servo's signal wire can connect to a GPIO pin, but its power comes from 5 V (VBUS for one small servo, a separate supply for anything bigger), never from a GPIO pin.
  • If anything gets hot or smells, unplug it immediately and look for a short before plugging back in.
  • Keep drinks off the desk, and touch something metal and grounded before handling a board on a dry day.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1The last line of a traceback says NameError: name 'sensor' isn't defined and points to line 9. What do you check first?

  • NameError means the name doesn't exist yet at that moment, usually a typo or an assignment that comes later.

  • A wiring mistake can't cause a NameError. Python failed before it ever touched a pin.

  • Memory problems raise MemoryError, not NameError.

Show answer

A. NameError means the name doesn't exist yet at that moment, usually a typo or an assignment that comes later.

2You want help with a project that connects to your home Wi-Fi. What's safe to put in a public Wokwi project?

  • Free projects are public, and the gateway is monitored. Treat anything in the project as published.

  • The simulated board only needs the open virtual network, so there is no secret to leak.

  • Every file in a public project is just as visible as main.py.

Show answer

B. The simulated board only needs the open virtual network, so there is no secret to leak.

Key takeaways

  • Save with a free account (public), a downloaded ZIP, or by copying files; keep one local folder per project.
  • Read a traceback from the bottom: error type and message, then the line number.
  • Debug in order: traceback, a print before the pin line, pin number, part orientation and power.
  • Never put real passwords or personal details in a Wokwi project. Real hardware rules: unplug to rewire, 3.3 V only on GPIO, resistors on LEDs, drivers for motors.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Navigate with pwd, ls, and cd, and predict where a relative path leads.
  • Create, edit, copy, and delete files, knowing which commands can't be undone.
  • Read a permission string like -rwxr-x---, fix "Permission denied", and use sudo only when it's needed.
  • Convert between physical pin numbers and GPIO numbers on a Raspberry Pi and a Pico W.
  • Keep GPIO connections at 3.3 V and inside the current limits of each board.

A setup guide for a temperature sensor says: "Connect the sensor's data wire to pin 17, then run sudo cp sensor.conf /boot/firmware/config.txt." Both halves of that sentence can wreck your afternoon.

On a Raspberry Pi, physical pin 17 is a 3.3 V power pin. The guide meant GPIO17, which lives at physical pin 11. And that cp command silently replaces the file the Pi reads every time it boots, with no undo. Neither mistake produces an error message. The fix is the same for both: know exactly which numbering and which file a command refers to before you press Enter.

#Where am I? The prompt, pwd, ls, and cd

The terminal is a conversation. You type a command, press Enter, and the computer prints a reply. The commands in this lesson work in any Linux terminal: a Raspberry Pi over SSH, the Linux environment on a Chromebook, Ubuntu under WSL on Windows (run wsl --install in PowerShell to get it), or the macOS Terminal, which behaves almost the same.

pwd (print working directory) says where you are. ls lists what's here. cd changes directory. Linux has one tree of folders starting at /, the root, and your own files live in your home folder, /home/student, which you can always write as ~.

A path that starts with / is absolute: it means the same place no matter where you are. Any other path is relative to where you are now. Two special names help: . means "this folder" and .. means "the folder above". Watch how the shell resolves a relative path one piece at a time:

.. removed iot-lab, . changed nothing, and the other names were added on. Press Tab while typing a path and the shell completes it for you, which also catches typos before they cause trouble. The Up arrow brings back your previous commands.

#Commands that change files, and the ones you can't undo

Three of these deserve respect. cp and mv overwrite an existing file with the same name without asking, and rm deletes immediately. There is no recycle bin. Adding -i (cp -i, mv -i, rm -i) makes them ask first, which is a good habit when you're working near files you care about. When you're unsure what a command does, man cp shows its manual (press q to leave), and most commands also accept --help.

#sudo, apt, and why you shouldn't sudo everything

Your account can change your own files. System files, such as installed programs and boot settings, belong to the administrator account, root. sudo runs one command as root after asking for your password:

apt is the package manager on Raspberry Pi OS, Debian, and Ubuntu. Run sudo apt update first so it knows about the newest versions. Use sudo only for commands that really change the system. Running your own scripts with sudo "to make the error go away" gives every bug in them the power to damage the whole system.

#Permissions: who can read, write, and run a file

ls -l shows the details:

The first column packs in a lot. The first character is d for a directory or - for a file. Then come three groups of three: what the owner can do, what the group can do, and what everyone else can do. In each group, r means read, w means write, x means execute (run a program, or enter a directory), and - means no.

Each group is also a digit: read is 4, write is 2, run is 1, added together. So rwxr-x--- is 750, and chmod 750 file sets exactly that. You'll use this in Module 7, where a file holding a device password should be readable by its owner only (600).

The permission error you'll meet first comes from running a script you just wrote:

New files aren't executable. Either run it through Python with python3 logger.py, or mark it as a program with chmod +x logger.py (and give it a first line of #!/usr/bin/env python3 so the system knows which interpreter to use).

#Physical pins versus GPIO numbers

Both boards in this course number their pins twice. Physical (board) numbers count positions on the connector. GPIO numbers are the chip's names for the signals, and they're what code uses. They almost never match:

On a real Pi, the pinout command (installed with gpiozero on Raspberry Pi OS) prints this map in the terminal. gpiozero accepts either style if you're explicit: LED(17) and LED("GPIO17") mean GPIO17, while LED("BOARD11") means physical pin 11, which is the same wire. On the Pico W, code uses GP numbers (Pin(15) is GP15 at physical pin 20), and the drawing in Wokwi labels them.

#Electrical limits: 3.3 V logic and a small current budget

A GPIO pin set high outputs 3.3 V, and a pin used as an input expects somewhere between 0 and 3.3 V. Neither board's GPIO pins tolerate 5 V. The RP2040 chip on the Pico W is rated for at most 0.5 V above its 3.3 V supply on any pin, and Raspberry Pi's documentation warns that 5 V on a GPIO can permanently damage the processor. Many sensors sold for Arduino run at 5 V and output 5 V signals. Those need a level shifter or a voltage divider (two resistors that scale the voltage down) before they touch a GPIO pin.

Current is the other limit. Each pin can only supply a little, and the whole chip has a total budget:

Per pin All GPIO pins together
Raspberry Pi 4 / 5 up to 16 mA 50 mA
Pico W (RP2040) 4 mA at the default drive setting (adjustable from 2 to 12 mA) 50 mA sourced

A series resistor sets an LED's current. Ohm's law says the current is the voltage left over after the LED, divided by the resistance:

330 Ω gives about 4 mA, which is why the circuits in this course use it. Motors, relays, and long LED strips need far more than any pin can give, so they always go through a driver or transistor with their own supply.

⚠️ Watch out

Three mistakes that fail silently. Wiring to the physical pin number when the guide meant the GPIO number (pin 17 versus GPIO17). Feeding a 5 V sensor output straight into a GPIO pin; it may even work for a while before the pin dies. And on Raspberry Pi OS, trying sudo pip install to fix a missing library: modern versions refuse with error: externally-managed-environment. Install the Debian package instead (sudo apt install python3-gpiozero), or create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv.

4 questions

1You're in /home/student/iot-lab/logs. Where does cd ../../projects take you?

  • That needs only one ... Each .. climbs one level, and there are two.

  • The first .. leaves logs, the second leaves iot-lab, then projects is added.

  • Only an absolute path (starting with /) would jump to the root.

Show answer

B. The first .. leaves logs, the second leaves iot-lab, then projects is added.

2ls -l shows -rw-r----- 1 student iot 120 settings.env. Who can read the file?

  • The owner group is rw- and the group's is r--; everyone else gets ---.

  • Read and execute are separate permissions. The last three characters, ---, deny everything to others.

  • The middle group r-- gives the iot group read access too.

Show answer

A. The owner group is rw- and the group's is r--; everyone else gets ---.

3A tutorial says "connect the button to pin 12" on a Raspberry Pi and its code says Button(12). What's the problem?

  • Physical pin 12 is GPIO18. GPIO12 is at physical pin 32.

  • Always check which numbering a guide uses. Button("BOARD12") would mean physical pin 12.

  • Any GPIO pin can read a button.

Show answer

B. Always check which numbering a guide uses. Button("BOARD12") would mean physical pin 12.

4A distance sensor runs on 5 V and its output pin swings between 0 and 5 V. How should it connect to a Pico W?

  • Analog pins are still 3.3 V pins. 5 V on them can damage the chip.

  • VBUS is a 5 V power pin; connecting a signal there does nothing useful, and code can't read it.

Show answer

B. That keeps the pin inside its rating while still letting the Pico W see the signal change.

Key takeaways

  • pwd, ls, and cd move you around; .. goes up one folder and ~ is your home folder.
  • cp, mv, and rm can destroy files without asking; add -i when it matters.
  • Use sudo for system changes such as apt install, never as a fix for your own script's errors.
  • rwx triplets for owner, group, and others; chmod +x makes a script runnable, and 600 locks a file to its owner.
  • Code uses GPIO numbers, not physical pin positions. GPIO pins are 3.3 V only, and each has a small current budget.

  • Ubuntu's command line for beginners (opens in a new tab): a free, hands-on tutorial covering the same commands with more practice.
  • pinout.xyz (opens in a new tab): an interactive Raspberry Pi header map; click any pin to see its GPIO number and alternate functions.
  • gpiozero's pin numbering notes (opens in a new tab): the start of the recipes page explains GPIO versus BOARD numbering with a diagram.

m2-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a project folder and files from the Linux terminal.
  • Describe a circuit as a CSV wiring plan with one row per part.
  • Write checks for pin names, analog-capable pins, reused pins, signal voltage, and LED current.
  • Wire the approved plan in Wokwi and confirm each part with a short test program.
  • Make the checker an executable command on Linux with a shebang and chmod +x.

Engineers don't solder first and test later. They write the plan down, check it against the datasheet, and only then pick up a wire. You'll do the same for the circuit Module 3 programs: two LEDs, a button, a knob, and a light sensor on a Pico W.

The tool you build reads a plan like the one below and refuses it, with reasons, if any connection would fail or damage the board. Then you'll fix the plan, wire it in Wokwi, and run a test that exercises every part.

#Step 1: Make the project folder

On any Linux terminal (a Raspberry Pi over SSH, WSL, a Chromebook, or macOS Terminal):

touch creates empty files. Both are readable and writable by you, and neither is executable yet; Step 7 changes that. If you don't have a terminal handy, the Python cells on this page work the same way: the first one writes plan.csv and later ones read it.

#Step 2: Write the plan as CSV

Each row is one part: its name, the Pico W pin its signal uses, what kind of connection it is, the highest voltage the signal can reach, and for LEDs the resistor and the LED's forward voltage. This first draft has four mistakes in it. See if you can spot them before the checker does.

#Step 3: Load the plan and check pin names

csv.DictReader turns each row into a dictionary keyed by the header, which keeps the checks readable. The Pico W's usable GPIO pins are GP0 to GP22 plus GP26 to GP28, and only those last three can read analog voltages.

GP22 is a perfectly good digital pin, but a potentiometer produces a voltage anywhere between 0 and 3.3 V, and GP22 can only tell "high" from "low". The knob would read as a switch.

#Step 4: Catch a pin used twice

Two parts on one pin fight each other: two outputs drive against each other, and an input next to an output reads whatever the output is doing. collections.Counter counts how many rows claim each pin.

#Step 5: Reject signals above 3.3 V

The light sensor in the draft is a 5 V module. Its output can reach 5 V, which is above what any Pico W pin survives.

#Step 6: Add up the LED currents

Each LED's current is the voltage left after the LED, divided by its resistor. The checker warns above the Pico W's default 4 mA drive setting (the pin's voltage sags and the LED is dimmer than the math says), refuses anything above 12 mA, and refuses a total above the chip's 50 mA budget.

#Step 7: The finished checker

Here is the whole tool in one file. It runs every check, prints a report, and returns 0 when the plan is safe and 1 when it isn't, the convention every Linux command uses for success and failure. This cell runs it on the draft, then on a corrected plan:

The fixes: the alarm LED got a 330 Ω resistor, the knob moved to GP26, the light sensor is now powered from 3V3 so its output can't pass 3.3 V, and the fan LED was dropped because GP15 was already taken. If you need a third LED, give it its own pin.

To use the checker as a terminal command, save the program in pincheck.py, then make two small changes: a first line that names the interpreter, and a last line that takes the file name from the command line instead of hard-coding it.

echo $? prints the exit status of the last command. Scripts and automated tests use that number to decide whether to carry on, which is why the checker returns it instead of only printing.

#Step 8: Wire the approved plan in Wokwi

Start a new Micropython Pico W project, open diagram.json, and replace its contents with the approved plan:

Both sensors are powered from pico:3V3, never from VBUS, exactly as the checker demanded. The button connects GP13 to ground when pressed, and "key": "b" lets you press it by holding B.

#Step 9: Smoke-test every part

A smoke test checks that each part responds at all, before you write real logic around it. Put this in main.py and press play:

Each LED should flash once, then a line prints twice a second. Click the knob and press Home and End: its number should swing from near 0 to near 65535. Hold B: the button value drops from 1 to 0. Click the light sensor while the simulation runs and drag its lux slider; brighter light gives a lower number, because of how that module is wired. If any part doesn't respond, the plan and the wiring disagree somewhere, and the smoke test has just saved you from debugging it inside a bigger program.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the checker reject the knob on GP22 even though GP22 is a valid GPIO pin?

  • GP22 can be an input; it just can only read high or low.

  • A potentiometer's output is a range of voltages, so it needs a pin connected to the analog-to-digital converter.

  • The Wi-Fi chip uses internal pins that aren't on the edge connector; GP22 is free.

Show answer

B. A potentiometer's output is a range of voltages, so it needs a pin connected to the analog-to-digital converter.

2Why does main return 1 for a bad plan instead of just printing the problems?

  • By convention 0 means success and anything else means failure, so ./pincheck.py plan.csv && echo build it only continues for a safe plan.

  • Functions without a return simply return None.

  • The checker runs on your computer and never touches the board.

Show answer

A. By convention 0 means success and anything else means failure, so ./pincheck.py plan.csv && echo build it only continues for a safe plan.

3The light sensor runs on 5 V in the draft. Which fix did the plan use?

  • GP28 is also a 3.3 V pin; moving the wire doesn't change the voltage.

  • A resistive sensor's output can't exceed its supply, so powering it from 3.3 V keeps the signal in range.

  • That silences the check without making the circuit any safer.

Show answer

B. A resistive sensor's output can't exceed its supply, so powering it from 3.3 V keeps the signal in range.

Key takeaways

  • Write the wiring down as data, then check it with code, before touching a wire.
  • Pins must exist, analog parts need GP26 to GP28, and no two parts share a pin.
  • Every signal stays at or below 3.3 V; power sensors from 3V3.
  • Size LED resistors for about 4 mA per pin and keep the total far below 50 mA.
  • A shebang, chmod +x, and a meaningful exit status turn a Python file into a real command.
  • Smoke-test each part with a tiny program before writing the real logic.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a servo kind that must use a PWM-capable pin and must be powered from VBUS or an external 5 V supply, never 3V3.
  • Make the checker also print the physical pin number for each GP pin, so you can wire a real board from its report.
  • Read a second column, pull, and warn when a button has no pull-up or pull-down.

#Further reading

  • Python's csv module (opens in a new tab): DictReader, DictWriter, and the quirks of quoting.
  • SparkFun's voltage divider tutorial (opens in a new tab): how to bring a 5 V signal down to 3.3 V with two resistors, with worked examples.
  • Raspberry Pi Pico W datasheet (opens in a new tab): the pin table this checker's rules come from.

m2-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Predict the result of a sequence of cd commands, including .. and ~.
  • Convert between permission strings and chmod numbers, and pick the right permissions for scripts, logs, and secrets.
  • Diagnose four common terminal errors from their exact messages.
  • Audit a wiring list against the Raspberry Pi header and flag power pins used as signals.
  • Size LED resistors for 3.3 V and design a voltage divider for a 5 V sensor.

These exercises go from quick predictions to small tools you'll reuse. Try each one on paper or in your head first, then open the solution. The Python solutions run right on this page.

Warm-up. Which of these paths mean the same place no matter where you are: /etc/hosts, logs/today.csv, ~/iot-lab, ../plan.csv? (Answer: /etc/hosts and ~/iot-lab. The shell expands ~ to your home folder's absolute path before the command sees it. The other two depend on your current folder.)

#Exercise 1: Where does this land?

Your home folder is /home/student. Predict what the last command prints, then write a small Python function that follows cd commands and check your answer.

Need a hint?

mkdir doesn't move you. After cd iot-lab/m3 you're in /home/student/iot-lab/m3. Then go into logs, up one, up one more.

Show solution

logs/../.. goes into logs, back out to m3, then up to iot-lab. The if parts: guard copies a real shell rule: cd .. at / stays at /.

#Exercise 2: Permissions for three kinds of file

Write to_string("640") that turns a chmod number into a permission string like rw-r-----. Then choose a number for each file:

  1. logger.py: you edit and run it; nobody else should touch it.
  2. readings.csv: you write it; your group (the dashboard account) reads it.
  3. device.env: holds a password; only you may read or change it.
Need a hint?

Each digit is a sum: read 4, write 2, run 1. So rw- is 4 + 2 = 6 and r-- is 4. Loop over the three digits and build three characters for each.

Show solution

value & 4 tests whether the 4 bit is set in that digit. The secrets file gets no group or "others" access at all, which is the rule Module 7 relies on: a credential file should be 600.

#Exercise 3: Read four terminal errors

For each message, say what went wrong and give the command that fixes it.

Need a hint?

Two of these are about permissions, but they need very different fixes. For the last one, look closely at the \r: what kind of computer adds that to the end of every line?

Show solution
  1. The file isn't executable. Run chmod +x pincheck.py, or run it as python3 pincheck.py.
  2. /etc belongs to root. sudo cp would work, but first ask whether the file belongs there at all. A project's settings can live in ~/iot-lab, which needs no special rights. Use sudo only when a system service really reads from /etc.
  3. A typo: the command is python3. Press the Up arrow, fix it, and press Enter.
  4. The file was saved with Windows line endings, so the first line ends in a hidden carriage return (\r) and the system looks for a program literally called python3\r. Convert it with sed -i 's/\r$//' pincheck.py, or set your editor to save with LF line endings.

#Exercise 4: Audit a wiring list for a Raspberry Pi

A tutorial lists its connections by physical pin. Write audit(wires) that prints what each physical pin really is and flags any signal wire landing on a power or ground pin.

Need a hint?

Use a dictionary from physical pin to name, like the one in the notes. A wire is suspicious if its name doesn't contain "ground" but the pin is 3V3, 5V, or GND.

Show solution

The tutorial almost certainly meant GPIO17 for the sensor, but GPIO17 already drives the LED. The honest fix is to choose a free GPIO pin, such as GPIO22 at physical pin 15, and update both the wire and the code.

#Exercise 5: LED resistors on a 3.3 V pin

Aim for about 4 mA per LED from a 3.3 V pin. Find the smallest standard resistor (10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82, times 1, 10, or 100) that keeps the current at or below 4 mA for a red LED (2.0 V), a green LED (2.2 V), and a blue LED (3.0 V). Then explain why the blue LED is a bad idea on 3.3 V.

Need a hint?

The ideal resistance is (3.3 − LED voltage) / 0.004. Walk through the standard values from smallest to largest and stop at the first one that's at least that big. For the blue LED, try a forward voltage of 2.9 V and of 3.2 V; real LEDs from one bag vary that much.

Show solution

With only 0.3 V left over, small differences between LEDs swing the current from about 5 mA to about 1 mA, so one blue LED glows and its neighbor looks dead. Blue and white LEDs need a higher supply and a transistor, or a red, green, or yellow LED instead.

#Exercise 6: A voltage divider for a 5 V sensor

A sensor's output swings from 0 to 5 V. A divider uses two resistors: R1 from the sensor's output to the GPIO pin, and R2 from the pin to ground. The pin sees 5 × R2 / (R1 + R2). Using standard values between 1 kΩ and 82 kΩ, list pairs whose output lands between 3.0 V and 3.3 V, with a total resistance of at least 10 kΩ so the divider doesn't load the sensor much. Print the five closest to 3.2 V.

Need a hint?

Loop over every R1 and every R2 from the standard list, compute the output, keep the pairs that pass both tests, then sort them by abs(volts - 3.2). Watch out: 10k and 20k gives 3.33 V, a hair too high.

Show solution

Many pairs work because only the ratio matters: R2 needs to be a bit under twice R1. The minimum total keeps the divider from drawing much current from the sensor. A divider only works for signals going into the Pico W, and it's too slow for very fast signals; a level-shifter chip handles those.

#Challenge: Catch PWM pins that can't work together

On the Pico W's RP2040 chip, PWM comes from 8 slices, each with two channels, A and B. GPIO pin n uses slice (n // 2) % 8 and channel A if n is even, B if odd. Two rules follow: pins on the same slice must run at the same frequency, and pins on the same slice and channel always get the same duty cycle, so they can't be controlled separately.

Write pwm_conflicts(outputs) for a list of (part, pin_number, frequency_hz) and report every broken rule. Test it with a servo on GP16 at 50 Hz, a status LED on GP17 at 1000 Hz, and a fan LED on GP0 at 50 Hz.

Need a hint?

Compute (slice, channel) for each output. Compare every pair with two nested loops (or itertools.combinations): same slice with different frequencies is one problem; same slice and channel is the other.

Show solution

GP16 and GP17 are neighbors, so they share slice 0; the servo needs 50 Hz while LEDs usually run much faster, and one slice can't do both. GP0 is slice 0 channel A, exactly like GP16, and it drags the status LED into a third conflict. Moving both LEDs to GP14 and GP15 (slice 7, both at 1000 Hz) leaves the servo alone on its slice, which is the layout Module 3 uses.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why an unconnected input reads randomly, and fix it with a pull-up resistor.
  • Detect a button press as an edge and ignore contact bounce.
  • Convert read_u16() values into volts, percentages, and a temperature, and reject readings that can't be true.
  • Use PWM duty cycle to set LED brightness and servo angle.
  • Schedule a blink, a sensor reading, and a button check in one loop with ticks_ms and ticks_diff.

Your environmental station blinks a status LED, reads a temperature every two seconds, and has a button to change modes. The obvious code is led.toggle() followed by time.sleep(1). Then you notice the button only works if you press it at exactly the right moment, because for 99.9% of every second the board is asleep and not looking.

Every idea in this lesson leads to the same habit: read the inputs, update the outputs, and get back to the top of the loop quickly.

#Digital inputs: why a loose wire reads random values

A pin set as an input reports whether the voltage on it is near 3.3 V (1) or near 0 V (0). A button connects a pin to something only while it's pressed. When it's released, the pin is connected to nothing at all, and an unconnected input "floats": it picks up electrical noise and reads 0 or 1 unpredictably.

A pull-up resistor fixes that by connecting the pin weakly to 3.3 V. Released, the pin reads 1. Pressed, the button connects the pin straight to ground, which overpowers the weak resistor, and the pin reads 0. The RP2040 has pull-ups built in, so you switch one on in code:

This is called active low: pressed means 0. It looks backwards at first, but it's the most common way to wire buttons, because the button only needs a wire to ground. Pin.PULL_DOWN does the opposite for a button wired to 3V3.

#Edges and bounce: counting one press as one press

You usually care about the moment the button goes down, not the whole time it's held. That moment is an edge: the value changed from 1 to 0 since the last check. Real buttons make it harder. Their metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, so one press can look like several quick presses. Wokwi simulates this bounce too.

The fix is debouncing: accept a new level only after it has stayed the same for a few readings in a row. Step through this simulation, where each number is one reading taken 5 ms apart, and compare the two counters:

The naive counter saw two presses, because the contacts bounced between the third and fifth readings. The debounced version only changed its mind once the level had held for three readings (15 ms), so it counted one.

#Analog inputs: from a voltage to a number

GP26, GP27, and GP28 connect to the RP2040's analog-to-digital converter (ADC), which measures a voltage between 0 and 3.3 V. In MicroPython, read_u16() reports it as a number from 0 to 65535. The chip really measures in 4,096 steps (12 bits), and MicroPython scales that up to the 16-bit range so the same code works on boards with different converters.

A potentiometer wired between 3V3 and GND turns its knob position into exactly this kind of voltage. On the board it's one line, ADC(Pin(26)).read_u16(). Real readings jitter by a few counts even when nothing moves, so programs often average several readings before using them; you'll practise that in lesson 3.

#The onboard temperature sensor, and a reading you shouldn't trust

The RP2040 also has a fifth ADC channel wired to a temperature sensor inside the chip. Raspberry Pi's datasheet gives the conversion: the sensor outputs about 0.706 V at 27 °C, and the voltage falls by 1.721 mV for every degree warmer.

Run that in Wokwi and you'll most likely get about 437 °C. Wokwi's Pi Pico documentation notes that its simulated temperature sensor always reads 0, and here's what the formula does with that:

Newer firmware also accepts ADC(ADC.CORE_TEMP), which picks the right channel on any RP2 chip. A real Pico W gives a sensible number, but it measures the chip, which runs warmer than the room, and each chip is a little different. Treat it as a "board is overheating" alarm, not a weather reading. The bigger lesson applies to every sensor in this course: check readings against what's physically possible before you log them or act on them. A sensor that says 437 °C is broken, unwired, or simulated, and your code should say so.

#PWM: in-between outputs from a pin that's only on or off

A GPIO pin can only output 0 V or 3.3 V. Pulse-width modulation (PWM) switches it on and off hundreds or thousands of times a second. The fraction of each cycle spent on is the duty cycle. An LED switched fast enough looks steadily dimmer at lower duty cycles, because your eye averages the flicker.

In MicroPython, duty_u16 takes the duty cycle as a number from 0 (always off) to 65535 (always on):

A servo uses PWM differently. It expects a pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz), and the length of that pulse sets the angle. Common micro servos, and Wokwi's simulated one, move from 0° to 180° as the pulse grows from about 0.5 ms to 2.4 ms; check your servo's datasheet, because the ends vary. Converting an angle to duty_u16 is arithmetic you can check here:

So servo = PWM(Pin(16), freq=50) followed by servo.duty_u16(4751) points it to about 90°. MicroPython also has duty_ns(), which takes the pulse length in nanoseconds directly.

#Doing several things at once without blocking

time.sleep() freezes everything. The non-blocking alternative asks, on every pass of the loop, "is it time yet?" time.ticks_ms() returns a millisecond counter, and each job remembers when it last ran:

The loop runs roughly 200 times a second, so the button is checked every 5 ms while the LED and the knob keep their own schedules. Always subtract with ticks_diff(now, then), never now - then. The counter wraps back to zero after about 12 days on the Pico W, and ticks_diff handles the wrap correctly.

#The same ideas on a Raspberry Pi with gpiozero

On the Pico W (MicroPython) On a Raspberry Pi (gpiozero)
Pin(13, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP) Button(13) (pull-up on by default; button.is_pressed, when_pressed)
PWM(Pin(15), freq=1000) and duty_u16() PWMLED(15) and led.value = 0.25
PWM(Pin(16), freq=50) and a pulse length AngularServo(16, min_angle=0, max_angle=180, min_pulse_width=0.0005, max_pulse_width=0.0024) and servo.angle = 90
ADC(Pin(26)).read_u16() No built-in analog inputs: add an ADC chip such as the MCP3008 and use MCP3008(channel=0).value

gpiozero runs callbacks like when_pressed in the background, so on a Pi you often don't write the polling loop yourself. The rule about not blocking still applies to whatever your own code does.

⚠️ Watch out

Classic bugs in this lesson. A button with no pull-up gives random presses: add Pin.PULL_UP. Code that reads the button only after a sleep(1) misses presses: use the ticks pattern. A servo powered from 3V3 twitches or resets the board: power it from VBUS or a separate 5 V supply and connect only its signal wire to GPIO. And a sensor reading of 437 °C (or 0, or 65535 forever) usually means a wiring or simulation problem, not weather.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A button is wired between GP13 and GND with Pin.PULL_UP. What does button.value() return while it's held down?

  • 1 is the released state; the pull-up holds the pin high when nothing else is connected.

  • Pressing connects the pin directly to ground, which overpowers the weak pull-up.

  • That's what a floating input does. The pull-up is there to prevent it.

Show answer

B. Pressing connects the pin directly to ground, which overpowers the weak pull-up.

2read_u16() on a potentiometer returns 49152. Roughly what voltage is on the pin?

  • That's half of 3.3 V, which would read about 32768.

  • 49152 is three quarters of 65535, and three quarters of 3.3 V is about 2.48 V.

  • The ADC can't measure above 3.3 V, and the pin must never see that much.

Show answer

B. 49152 is three quarters of 65535, and three quarters of 3.3 V is about 2.48 V.

3You want a servo at 0°. With pulses from 0.5 ms (0°) to 2.4 ms (180°) at 50 Hz, which duty is right?

  • 0.5 ms out of a 20 ms period is 2.5%, and 2.5% of 65535 is about 1638.

  • A duty of 0 sends no pulses at all, so the servo receives no position command.

  • That's 50% duty, a 10 ms pulse, far outside what a servo expects.

Show answer

A. 0.5 ms out of a 20 ms period is 2.5%, and 2.5% of 65535 is about 1638.

4Why use time.ticks_diff(now, last) instead of now - last?

  • Speed isn't the reason; both are tiny operations.

  • After about 12 days ticks_ms() restarts near zero, so plain subtraction would suddenly go negative.

  • It runs fine. It just gives wrong answers after the wrap, which is worse.

Show answer

B. After about 12 days ticks_ms() restarts near zero, so plain subtraction would suddenly go negative.

Key takeaways

  • Inputs need a defined level: use Pin.PULL_UP and read 0 as "pressed".
  • React to edges, and debounce by waiting for a level to stay steady.
  • read_u16() maps 0 to 3.3 V onto 0 to 65535; only GP26 to GP28 (and channel 4, the chip's temperature) can do it.
  • Sanity-check every reading against what's physically possible.
  • PWM duty cycle sets brightness; a 50 Hz pulse of 0.5 to 2.4 ms sets a servo's angle.
  • Never block the main loop: give each job its own ticks_ms timer and compare with ticks_diff.

#Further reading

  • SparkFun on pull-up resistors (opens in a new tab): what floating inputs look like and how to choose an external pull-up.
  • SparkFun on pulse-width modulation (opens in a new tab): duty cycle, frequency, and examples beyond LEDs.
  • MicroPython's machine.ADC reference (opens in a new tab): read_u16, read_uv, and how each port numbers its channels.

m3-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Add a servo to a Wokwi circuit and power it correctly.
  • Test conversion functions in regular Python before they go on the board.
  • Drive LED brightness and servo angle from analog readings with PWM.
  • Switch modes on a debounced button press without missing presses.
  • Run a heartbeat, an alarm blink, and a status report on separate ticks_ms timers.

A greenhouse monitor needs to show its state at a glance, even to someone who never opens a dashboard. Here you'll build a panel that does that from the circuit you checked and wired in Module 2, plus one servo.

When it's finished:

  • Turning the knob dims or brightens the green status LED.
  • A servo needle acts as a gauge, showing either the knob position or the light level.
  • The blue button switches the gauge between those two modes.
  • The red alarm LED flashes quickly whenever the light falls below 20%.
  • The onboard LED blinks once a second as a heartbeat, so you can see the loop is alive, and the Serial Monitor prints a status line every second:

Your numbers will differ with the knob position and the simulated light level.

#Step 1: Add the servo to the circuit

Start from a new Micropython Pico W project and paste this into diagram.json. It's the Module 2 circuit plus a servo, whose signal uses GP16 and whose power comes from VBUS (5 V from USB), never from 3V3 or a GPIO pin.

The servo sits on GP16 for a reason you met in the Module 2 challenge: GP16 is on PWM slice 0, while the status LED on GP15 is on slice 7. The servo needs 50 Hz and the LED runs at 1000 Hz, and two pins on one slice can't have different frequencies.

#Step 2: Write the math first, and test it off the board

Testing on a microcontroller is slow: edit, run, squint at the terminal. So put every conversion in a small function and test it in regular Python first. These are the exact functions that go into main.py:

The clamping in angle_to_duty matters more than it looks. A bug that asks for 500° would otherwise send a pulse far outside the servo's range, and a real servo would grind against its end stop.

#Step 3: The knob dims the status LED

On the board, the LED becomes a PWM object, and each pass of the loop copies the knob's percentage into its duty cycle:

At 1000 Hz the flicker is far too fast to see. Wokwi's LEDs also mimic how eyes respond to light, so the bottom quarter of the knob's travel changes the brightness more visibly than the top quarter, just as a real LED does.

#Step 4: The servo becomes a gauge needle

0% points the needle to 0° and 100% to 180°. Setting the same duty again on every pass is harmless: the PWM hardware keeps producing the pulse on its own, and writing a new number only changes the next pulse.

#Step 5: A button that changes mode once per press

The button should flip the mode on the press, once, no matter how long it's held and no matter how much the contacts bounce. This function returns True only when the button has just settled into the pressed state:

It's the same idea as the trace in the notes, but measured in milliseconds instead of readings: any change restarts the clock, and the new level only counts once it has held for 30 ms. Releasing the button also updates stable_level, but returns False, so only presses switch the mode.

#Step 6: Timers for the alarm, the heartbeat, and the report

Each periodic job gets its own "last ran" time. The alarm flashes every 125 ms while it's dark and switches off the moment it isn't; the heartbeat and the status line run once a second. Here is the whole program. Paste it into main.py and press play:

Now test it like a user would. Click the knob and use the arrow keys or Home and End; the green LED and the needle follow. Hold B for a moment: mode -> light prints once, not five times. Click the light sensor and drag its lux slider down to about 10 lux: the light reading drops below 20%, the red LED flashes, and the needle (in light mode) swings low. Throughout, the heartbeat keeps its steady one-second rhythm, which proves nothing in the loop is blocking.

🧪 Try it yourself

Add time.sleep(1) just before time.sleep_ms(5) and run it again. The needle lags, the alarm flashes slowly, and quick button taps are missed. Take it out again.

#Step 7 (optional): The same panel on a Raspberry Pi

A Raspberry Pi has no analog inputs, so the knob and the light sensor connect through an MCP3008 ADC chip on the SPI pins (turn on SPI in sudo raspi-config under Interface Options). gpiozero handles the debouncing and the button callback for you. These pin choices avoid GPIO14 and GPIO15, which the Pi uses for its serial port:

Notice alarm_on: gpiozero's blink() starts a background blinker, so calling it on every pass would restart it 20 times a second. The variable makes sure it starts once when it gets dark and stops once when it gets light.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the servo use GP16 rather than GP17, the pin right next to it?

  • Every GPIO pin can produce PWM on the RP2040.

  • Two pins on one slice share a frequency. Using GP16 alone on its slice (with the LEDs on GP14 and GP15) avoids the clash.

  • VBUS is a separate power pin; the servo's signal can use any free GPIO.

Show answer

B. Two pins on one slice share a frequency. Using GP16 alone on its slice (with the LEDs on GP14 and GP15) avoids the clash.

2Why does the program read the knob on every pass but print only once a second?

  • The LED and needle need fresh values every few milliseconds, but a person can only read about one line a second.

  • The ADC can take hundreds of thousands of readings a second.

  • Printing and the ADC are unrelated.

Show answer

A. The LED and needle need fresh values every few milliseconds, but a person can only read about one line a second.

3What would happen if new_press returned True whenever button.value() == 0?

  • The mode would be checked on every pass of the loop, about 200 times a second.

  • The function must detect the moment of pressing, not the state of being pressed.

  • It would still work, just uncontrollably.

Show answer

B. The function must detect the moment of pressing, not the state of being pressed.

Key takeaways

  • Keep conversions in small functions and test them in regular Python before they reach the board.
  • PWM duty sets LED brightness at 1000 Hz and servo angle at 50 Hz; keep pins that need different frequencies on different slices.
  • Clamp anything that drives hardware, so a bug can't command an impossible position.
  • A debounced edge detector turns a bouncy, held-down button into exactly one event per press.
  • One fast loop with a ticks_ms timer per job keeps every output responsive; a heartbeat LED proves the loop is alive.

#Ideas to extend it

  • The needle jitters slightly as the ADC readings wobble. Only move the servo when the angle changes by more than 2°.
  • Add a third mode in which the needle sweeps slowly back and forth, one degree per 20 ms, without blocking.
  • Make a long press (over one second) reset the mode to knob.

#Further reading

  • MicroPython's machine.PWM reference (opens in a new tab): freq, duty_u16, duty_ns, and inverting outputs.
  • Wokwi's servo part (opens in a new tab): its pins, range of motion, and horn styles.
  • gpiozero output devices (opens in a new tab): PWMLED, AngularServo, and the background blink() behavior.

m3-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Map raw ADC readings to percentages with dead zones at the ends.
  • Reduce noise by averaging, and measure how much it helps.
  • Convert an NTC thermistor reading to °C and detect disconnected or shorted sensors.
  • Count button presses from timestamped samples with a settle time.
  • Use hysteresis so an alarm doesn't flicker near its threshold.
  • Compare tick counts correctly across a wrap-around, and move a servo gradually with a state machine.

Every exercise here is logic that runs on the Pico W, written as plain Python functions so you can test it on this page first. Each solution ends with a note on how to use it on the board.

Warm-up. In your head: what voltage does read_u16() = 20000 mean? (About 1.01 V: 20000 / 65535 × 3.3.) And what reading would 3.0 V give? (About 59577.)

#Exercise 1: A knob with dead zones

Real potentiometers rarely reach exactly 0 or 65535, so a "fully turned" knob might read 64,800 and never show 100%. Write knob_percent(raw) that returns 0 for anything at or below 1000, 100 for anything at or above 64500, and a straight line in between.

Need a hint?

Clamp first, then scale: (raw - LOW) / (HIGH - LOW) * 100 gives 0 at LOW and 100 at HIGH. Clamp the raw value into that range before the arithmetic.

Show solution

The midpoint of the usable range is 32750, not 32768, because the range itself starts at 1000. On the board, use knob_percent(knob.read_u16()) anywhere the status panel used percent().

#Exercise 2: How much does averaging help?

A sensor that should read 30000 comes back with random noise. Simulate 400 readings with random.gauss(30000, 400) (use random.seed(7) so your numbers match), then compare single readings with averages of 8 consecutive readings. Print the standard deviation of each.

Need a hint?

statistics.pstdev(values) gives the standard deviation. To make averages of 8, slice the list in steps: readings[i:i + 8] for i in range(0, 400, 8).

Show solution

Averaging n independent readings shrinks random noise by about √n, so 8 readings give roughly a 2.8× improvement and 64 would give 8×. On the board the helper is one line:

#Exercise 3: A thermistor that reports its own failures

Wokwi's NTC temperature sensor is a 10 kΩ thermistor in series with a 10 kΩ resistor, with a beta coefficient of 3950. Adapted for read_u16(), its documented formula is:

celsius = 1 / (log(1 / (65535 / raw - 1)) / 3950 + 1 / 298.15) - 273.15

Write ntc_celsius(raw) that returns the temperature rounded to one decimal, or None when the reading is impossible: a raw value of 0 or 65535 (the formula divides by zero or takes the log of zero there, which usually means a broken or shorted wire), or a result outside −40 to 125 °C.

Need a hint?

Check the two edge values before doing any math. Then compute, then check the range. Returning None lets the caller decide what to show, such as "sensor fault" instead of a fake number.

Show solution

In this module, the reading goes down as the temperature goes up. On the board, math.log exists in MicroPython too, so the same function works unchanged with ntc_celsius(ADC(Pin(28)).read_u16()). Module 7's failure planning builds on exactly this habit: a function that can say "I don't know" is safer than one that always returns a number.

#Exercise 4: Count presses from bouncy samples

These (time_ms, level) samples record two presses of a button with a pull-up (0 means pressed), with bounce on each press and release. Write count_presses(samples, settle_ms=20) that counts a press only when the level has been 0 for at least settle_ms since it last changed.

Need a hint?

Walk through the samples keeping level, changed_at, and a stable level. A new sample with a different level updates level and changed_at. Before applying each sample, check whether the current level has lasted settle_ms up to this sample's time; if so and it differs from stable, the stable level changes, and a change to 0 is a press.

Show solution

The level settles at 0 from 108 ms to 300 ms and from 603 ms to 900 ms, so there are two presses. The short blips at 303 ms and 600 ms never last 20 ms, so they're ignored. On the board, use the same rule with time.ticks_diff(now, changed_at) in place of the subtraction, as the status panel's new_press does.

#Exercise 5: Stop the alarm from chattering

At dusk the light level drifts around 20% with a little noise, and the status panel's alarm flickers on and off. Generate the light readings below, then compare a single threshold (alarm when below 20) with hysteresis: turn on below 18, and turn off only above 24. Count how many times each version switches, and plot both.

(Your switch counts depend on the random seed; with the code below they match these.)

Need a hint?

With hysteresis, the alarm has memory: if it's on, only a reading above 24 can turn it off; if it's off, only a reading below 18 can turn it on. Keep the current state in a variable and update it per reading.

Show solution

The gap between 18 and 24 is wider than the noise, so once the alarm turns on, noise alone can't turn it off. On the board, keep alarm as a global variable and run the same if/elif on each new reading.

#Exercise 6: Survive the tick counter wrapping

On the Pico W, time.ticks_ms() counts up to 2³⁰ − 1 and then wraps to 0 (about 12.4 days). Write ticks_diff(end, start) the way MicroPython defines it, then show that a timer started just before the wrap is computed correctly, while plain subtraction is wildly wrong.

Need a hint?

With PERIOD = 2 ** 30 and HALF = PERIOD // 2, the difference is ((end - start + HALF) % PERIOD) - HALF. That maps any raw difference into the range from −HALF to HALF − 1.

Show solution

A greenhouse monitor that runs for two weeks will hit the wrap. With plain subtraction, every timer in the loop would stop firing for the next 12 days. time.ticks_diff is built into MicroPython, so on the board you never write this yourself; you just never subtract ticks directly.

#Challenge: A vent that opens gradually without blocking

A servo opens a greenhouse vent. It should open to 90° when the temperature rises above 28 °C and close to 0° when it falls below 25 °C, moving 2° per 20 ms tick so it doesn't slam. Model it as a state machine with four states and write step(state, angle, temp) that returns the new (state, angle) for one tick. Simulate 3 seconds (150 ticks) with the temperature at 30 °C for the first second and 22 °C afterwards, printing each state change.

Need a hint?

Handle the temperature checks first (they can interrupt a movement), then the movement: OPENING adds 2 and becomes OPEN at 90; CLOSING subtracts 2 and becomes CLOSED at 0. Keep step free of any hardware calls so you can test it here.

Show solution

From 0° to 90° in 2° steps takes 45 ticks (ticks 0 to 44), or 0.9 s, and the angle printed with each change is the angle after that tick's step. On the board, call step once every 20 ms from the main loop using a ticks_ms timer, then send angle_to_duty(angle) to the servo; the rest of the loop keeps reading sensors and buttons the whole time the vent is moving.
