m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick a sampling interval from how fast the measured thing changes, and recognize aliasing.
  • Choose between ticks_ms, the real-time clock, and NTP for timestamps, and store time in UTC.
  • Estimate how long a CSV log fits in the Pico W's flash.
  • Smooth noisy readings with a moving average and an exponential moving average, and explain the lag each adds.
  • Package a reading as a JSON payload and buffer payloads through a network outage without silently losing them.

One reading tells you the greenhouse is 22.4 °C right now. It can't tell you whether that's normal, whether it's rising, or whether the heater failed at 3 a.m. Those answers come from a time series: the same measurement, taken repeatedly, each with the time it was taken.

Getting a time series right means making five decisions: how often to sample, which clock to trust, how to store the readings, how to deal with noise, and what to do when the network disappears for twenty minutes. This lesson takes them in that order.

#How often to sample, and what aliasing looks like

Sampling too slowly misses events. Sampling too fast fills storage, drains batteries, and floods the network with near-identical numbers. The right interval depends on the fastest change you care about.

Slow sampling can do worse than miss things: it can invent patterns that aren't there. Suppose a heater cycles on and off every 10 minutes, swinging the temperature by ±1.5 °C. Watch what readings every 9 minutes show:

The orange line is a slow, smooth wave that never happened. This effect is aliasing. The theory (the Nyquist rate) says you need more than two samples per cycle of the fastest change to capture it at all; in practice, engineers aim for five to ten. Room air changes over minutes, so a reading every 10 to 60 seconds is plenty. A vibration sensor might need thousands of readings per second.

#Which clock goes on each reading

The Pico W has more than one idea of "now", and they answer different questions:

Clock What it gives Good for Watch out
time.ticks_ms() Milliseconds since power-up Timers in the loop, measuring durations Restarts at 0 on every reboot; wraps after about 12 days
time.time(), time.gmtime() Calendar time from the board's clock Timestamps in logs Wrong until something sets it; a fresh board can think it's years in the past
ntptime.settime() Sets the board's clock to UTC from an internet time server Making time.time() correct after Wi-Fi connects Needs the network; check it worked before trusting timestamps

The pattern most IoT devices use: connect to Wi-Fi, set the clock with NTP, then stamp every reading with UTC. UTC never jumps for daylight saving, so 01:30 can't happen twice in one night. Convert to local time only when you display data. If NTP fails, record ticks_ms with the reading and mark the calendar time as unknown, rather than writing a wrong date that looks right.

#Logging to CSV, and how fast the flash fills

A CSV log stores one row per reading, with the units in the column names so nobody has to guess:

On the board, appending a row is open("log.csv", "a") and write(). The catch is space: the Pico W's MicroPython firmware leaves 848 KB of flash for files. Here's how long that lasts at different intervals:

At one reading every 2 seconds the board fills in about half a day. That's one reason devices send their data somewhere rather than keeping it all. Flash also wears out after many rewrites of the same block, so loggers collect several rows in memory and write them in one go rather than opening the file for every reading.

#Smoothing: moving averages and exponential averages

Here are 90 minutes of simulated readings with sensor noise and one glitch at minute 40:

A moving average of 5 is the mean of the last five readings. An exponential moving average (EMA) keeps one running value and nudges it a fraction alpha of the way toward each new reading:

smooth = smooth + alpha × (reading − smooth)

Step through it with a short series that includes a glitch:

The EMA only needs to remember one number, which makes it ideal on a microcontroller. Both kinds of smoothing pay for their calm with lag: the smoothed line reacts late to real changes.

Notice the glitch: neither average removes it; they spread it into a smaller bump that lasts several minutes. Impossible values should be rejected (as the thermistor function in Module 3 did) before smoothing. And log the raw readings, smoothing only for display or decisions, because smoothing can't be undone later.

#JSON payloads: readings that describe themselves

A CSV row only makes sense next to its header. When a reading travels alone over a network, it needs to carry its own labels. JSON does that with the same syntax as a Python dictionary:

The JSON is more than three times bigger, and that's usually worth it: any program can read it without knowing the column order, and adding a field later doesn't break old readers. MicroPython's json module has the same dumps and loads. The seq field is a counter that goes up by one with every reading, so the receiver can spot missing ones. Round values before sending: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in both Pythons, and those digits travel in the payload.

#When the network drops: buffer, don't lose

A device that sends each reading the moment it's taken loses every reading taken while Wi-Fi is down. The fix is store and forward: put each payload in a queue, send from the front of the queue when the network is up, and remove a payload only after the receiver confirms it.

Memory is limited, so the queue needs a maximum length, and you have to decide what happens when it's full. Dropping the oldest readings keeps the most recent picture accurate. This simulation runs a 40-minute outage at one reading a minute with two queue sizes:

With room for 60, nothing is lost. With room for 25, the 16 oldest readings from the outage are dropped (the queue also takes minute 60's reading before it can send), and because each reading has a seq number, the receiver can tell exactly which ones. A gap you can detect beats a gap nobody notices.

⚠️ Watch out

Time-series mistakes that hide in plain sight. Using ticks_ms() as the timestamp in a log, which restarts at zero after every reboot so rows from different days interleave. Logging local time, which repeats an hour each autumn. Smoothing before logging, so the raw data is gone. Writing the log file on every reading, which wears the flash. And a queue with no limit, which works fine in testing and runs out of memory during the first long outage.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A door sensor must notice a door opened for at least 4 seconds. Which sampling interval is the most sensible?

  • A 4-second opening could fall entirely between two readings and never be seen.

  • That gives about eight samples during the shortest event, comfortably above the two-per-event minimum.

  • It would work, but it creates 4,000 readings per event for no benefit.

Show answer

B. That gives about eight samples during the shortest event, comfortably above the two-per-event minimum.

2Why store 2026-11-16T14:03:20Z rather than the local time?

  • Local time jumps at daylight-saving changes; convert to local only for display.

  • The size is about the same; the problem is ambiguity.

  • It can; the issue is what's stored, not what's possible.

Show answer

A. Local time jumps at daylight-saving changes; convert to local only for display.

3An EMA with alpha = 0.3 is at 22.0 °C and the next reading is 25.0 °C. What is the new smoothed value?

  • That would be alpha = 1, which is no smoothing at all.

  • 22.0 + 0.3 × (25.0 − 22.0) = 22.9.

  • That's the plain average of the two values, which an EMA doesn't compute.

Show answer

B. 22.0 + 0.3 × (25.0 − 22.0) = 22.9.

4The queue holds 25 readings and a 40-minute outage produces 40. What should the device do with the extra 15?

  • A crash loses everything in memory, including the 25 readings you could have kept.

  • New readings describe the current state, so they're usually the most valuable; dropping them hides what's happening now.

  • The most recent data survives, and the receiver can see precisely which readings are missing.

Show answer

C. The most recent data survives, and the receiver can see precisely which readings are missing.

Key takeaways

  • Sample five to ten times faster than the quickest change you care about; too slow causes aliasing, too fast wastes space and power.
  • Timers use ticks_ms; log timestamps use UTC from a clock set by NTP, with "unknown" when it isn't set.
  • A 30-byte CSV row every 2 s fills the Pico W's 848 KB in about half a day; write rows in batches.
  • Moving averages and EMAs reduce noise but add lag; reject impossible values first and log the raw data.
  • JSON payloads carry their own labels; a seq counter lets the receiver detect missing readings.
  • Store and forward: queue every payload, delete only after confirmed delivery, and cap the queue by dropping the oldest.

#Further reading

  • MicroPython's time module (opens in a new tab): ticks_ms, ticks_diff, gmtime, and how each port's clock and epoch work.
  • pandas rolling windows (opens in a new tab): moving averages and other window calculations over time series.
  • Python's json module (opens in a new tab): dumps, loads, and options for compact or pretty output.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Connect a Pico W to Wi-Fi in Wokwi and set its clock with NTP, with a fallback when either fails.
  • Read a thermistor and a light sensor into timestamped readings with sequence numbers.
  • Append readings to a CSV file on the board's flash in batches, and copy the file off the board.
  • Test the queue logic in regular Python, including an outage, before deploying it.
  • Post batches of JSON readings over HTTP and remove them from the queue only after the server confirms.

In the last lesson's simulation, a queue kept every reading through a 40-minute outage. Now you'll build the real thing on a Pico W. The device reads temperature and light every 2 seconds, logs each reading to a file, and posts them in batches to a web server over Wi-Fi. A slide switch on the breadboard pretends to unplug the network, so you can watch the backlog grow, then drain without losing a single reading.

This is what the Serial Monitor shows around a simulated outage (your numbers will differ):

#Step 1: Wire the sensors and the outage switch

Start a new Micropython Pico W project and paste this into diagram.json:

The slide switch's middle pin goes to GP12 with a pull-up. Slid right (where "value": "1" starts it), nothing pulls GP12 down, so it reads 1 and the code treats the network as available. Slid left, it connects GP12 to ground, reads 0, and the code behaves as if the network were unplugged. That gives you an outage on demand without touching Wokwi's Wi-Fi.

#Step 2: Connect, set the clock, and take a reading

Each function does one job and fails gracefully. connect_wifi gives up after 15 seconds instead of hanging forever (remember that a Pico W retries a failed connection indefinitely unless you stop waiting). sync_clock asks an internet time server for UTC and reports whether it worked.

Two details matter later. time is None until the clock is set, so a reading never carries a believable but wrong date; up_ms is always there as a fallback. And temp_c uses Module 3's thermistor function, so a disconnected sensor shows up as None instead of a nonsense number.

#Step 3: Log to a CSV file in batches

Rows wait in a list and reach the flash five at a time. That's five times fewer writes, which matters for a device meant to run for months.

open(LOG) raises OSError when the file doesn't exist yet. That's how start_log decides whether to write the header, so restarting the program never adds a second header in the middle of the file.

#Step 4: Test the queue logic before it touches the board

The sending rules are where bugs hide: when to send, how much, what to delete. So test the exact same rules in regular Python first. Readings arrive every 2 seconds, a send is attempted every 6 seconds with up to 20 readings, the queue holds at most 100, and the link is down from 40 to 100 seconds:

Every reading arrives, in order, and the largest backlog (about 30) is far below the limit of 100. Plotting the backlog makes the outage visible:

Try changing MAX_BACKLOG to 20 and running both cells again: dropped becomes nonzero, and delivered is missing the oldest outage readings. That's the trade-off from the notes, now measured.

#Step 5: Post batches over HTTP

The board sends each batch as one JSON object to httpbin.org/post, a free public test service that replies with a copy of whatever it receives. A reply with status 200 is the confirmation; anything else, including an exception, means "keep the batch and try later."

Batching is the big efficiency win: one HTTP request carries 20 readings, instead of 20 requests each with their own connection setup. timeout=5 caps how long a stuck request can freeze the loop. A network call does block, which is why sends happen only every 6 seconds and why the sample timer, using ticks_diff, simply takes its next reading late rather than skipping it.

📝 Note

The readings travel through Wokwi's public gateway and a public test service, so they must never contain anything private. Fake greenhouse numbers are fine. MicroPython's requests encrypts an https:// connection, but by default it doesn't verify the server's certificate, so it can't prove who it's talking to. Module 6 deals with trusting the other end.

#Step 6: The finished logger

Put every piece together in main.py. The main loop has two timers: one takes a reading every 2 seconds, and the other attempts a send every 6 seconds and retries Wi-Fi and NTP if they failed at start-up.

Press play. After the Wi-Fi and clock messages, a reading prints every 2 seconds and a batch of about three goes out every 6. Now slide the switch left: offline messages appear, the backlog climbs, and the red LED stays on. After a minute, slide it right again. The next sends carry 20 readings at a time until the backlog is back to a handful.

To check the log, click in the Serial Monitor, press Ctrl+C, and type:

Every reading is there, including the ones taken while "offline", because logging happens before any attempt to send. Copy the output into a file on your computer for the next lesson's analysis. (On a real Pico W, mpremote cp :log.csv . copies the file directly.) Click the temperature sensor while the simulation runs and drag its slider to give yourself more interesting data.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the logger remove readings from the backlog only after send_batch returns True?

  • Speed isn't the concern. The order decides whether data can be lost.

  • Deleting only after the server confirms is what makes store and forward lossless.

  • requests knows nothing about your queue.

Show answer

B. Deleting only after the server confirms is what makes store and forward lossless.

2Why does each reading carry seq as well as time?

  • Sequence numbers count readings directly, so a gap from 41 to 57 is obvious whatever the timestamps say.

  • HTTP has no such rule. It's a choice made for the data.

  • Sorting isn't the purpose; detecting gaps is.

Show answer

A. Sequence numbers count readings directly, so a gap from 41 to 57 is obvious whatever the timestamps say.

3The log writes to flash every 5 readings instead of every reading. What's the trade-off?

  • If the power fails, up to four unwritten rows in memory are lost.

  • Real loggers pick the batch size from how valuable the newest data is versus how long the flash must last.

  • The CSV file stays on the board; it never goes over Wi-Fi.

Show answer

B. Real loggers pick the batch size from how valuable the newest data is versus how long the flash must last.

Key takeaways

  • Connect with a timeout, set the clock with NTP, and mark the time as unknown when that fails.
  • Every reading gets a seq number and an uptime, so gaps and order can be checked without trusting the clock.
  • Log first, send second: the local CSV file keeps every reading even when the network doesn't.
  • Batch both the flash writes and the HTTP posts; one request with 20 readings beats 20 requests.
  • Delete from the queue only after the server confirms; cap the queue and drop the oldest when it's full.
  • Test the queue rules in regular Python, with an outage, before running them on the board.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Save the backlog to a file whenever the link goes down, and reload it at start-up, so a reboot during an outage doesn't lose the queue.
  • Back off when sends fail: wait 6 s, then 12, then 24, up to a minute, so a broken server isn't hammered.
  • Send a reading immediately (instead of waiting for the batch) when the temperature changes by more than 2 °C since the last one sent.
  • Read the reply with resp.json() and check that httpbin echoed back the same seq numbers you sent.

#Further reading

  • MicroPython's network.WLAN reference (opens in a new tab): connecting, checking status, and the station and access-point modes.
  • Wokwi's WiFi networking guide (opens in a new tab): how the virtual Wokwi-GUEST network and the public gateway work. It's written for the ESP32, and the network is the same one your simulated Pico W joins.
  • MicroPython's mpremote tool (opens in a new tab): copying files to and from a real board, running scripts, and opening a REPL from your terminal.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Estimate how long a log fits in flash for CSV and JSON formats.
  • Summarize a CSV log while skipping empty and faulty values.
  • Find missing readings from sequence numbers and report each gap's length.
  • Pick an EMA strength by measuring both its noise and its lag.
  • Resample a time series into fixed buckets with pandas and spot incomplete buckets.
  • Validate incoming JSON payloads and explain each rejection.

The logger from the build-along produces exactly the kinds of files these exercises use. Every solution is regular Python that runs on this page; the same code would run on a Raspberry Pi or laptop that receives your device's data.

Warm-up. A device reads every 30 seconds. How many readings is that per day? (86,400 / 30 = 2,880.) If each JSON payload is about 110 bytes, how much data per day is that? (About 310 KB.)

#Exercise 1: CSV or JSON on the flash?

Write days_until_full(interval_s, row_bytes, flash_kb=848) and print how many days the Pico W's file space lasts at intervals of 5, 30, and 300 seconds, for 31-byte CSV rows and 106-byte JSON lines.

Need a hint?

Rows per day is 86400 / interval_s. Multiply by the row size to get bytes per day, then divide the flash size (in bytes) by that.

Show solution

JSON costs more than three times the space, which is why devices usually keep compact CSV locally and send JSON over the network, where the receiver stores it somewhere bigger. Even at one reading every 5 minutes, CSV fills the flash in under a year, so a long-running logger needs a plan for old data: delete what's been delivered, or keep only the latest days.

#Exercise 2: Summarize a log that has faults

This is logger output where the thermistor glitched once (an empty temp_c) and the light sensor once. Print how many valid temperatures there are, their minimum, maximum, and mean, and the seq numbers of rows with any missing value.

Need a hint?

csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(LOG)) reads a string as if it were a file. An empty cell arrives as the empty string "", so convert with float() only when the cell isn't empty.

Show solution

Notice what the code does not do: it never replaces a missing value with 0. A zero would drag the mean down to about 20.9 °C, a believable but false number. Skipping and reporting is the honest choice.

#Exercise 3: Find the gaps

A logger reading every 2 seconds sent these sequence numbers. Report each run of missing readings with its length in seconds, and the percentage of readings received.

Need a hint?

Walk through neighbouring pairs with zip(received, received[1:]). Whenever the next number isn't the previous plus one, the numbers in between are missing.

Show solution

Sequence numbers find gaps even when timestamps are missing or wrong. They can't see readings lost after the last one received, though; a receiver that also tracks "time since the last reading" catches a device that went silent, which Module 5's dashboard uses to mark data as stale.

#Exercise 4: How much smoothing?

A heater switches on at minute 30 and the true temperature steps from 20 °C to 25 °C. The sensor adds noise. For EMA strengths alpha of 0.1, 0.3, and 0.6, measure two things: the noise left in the smoothed signal (the standard deviation over minutes 10 to 29, when nothing is changing), and the lag (how many minutes after the step the smoothed value first reaches 24.5 °C, 90% of the way). Plot all three.

Need a hint?

Generate the data with NumPy: np.where(minutes < 30, 20.0, 25.0) plus rng.normal(0, 0.5, 60). Compute the EMA with a loop or pd.Series(raw).ewm(alpha=a, adjust=False).mean(). For the lag, find the first index at or after 30 where the smoothed value is at least 24.5.

Show solution

There's no free lunch: going from alpha 0.6 to 0.1 cuts the noise by more than half and makes the lag about seven times longer. For a greenhouse display, alpha 0.3 is a reasonable middle. For an alarm that must react fast, use light smoothing (or none) and rely on hysteresis instead, as in Module 3.

#Exercise 5: Five-minute summaries with pandas

Dashboards rarely plot every reading. Build an hour of readings taken every 30 seconds starting at 14:00 UTC, remove the readings from 14:20:00 to 14:27:30 to simulate an outage, then use pandas to summarize each 5-minute bucket with its mean, minimum, maximum, and count. Which buckets are incomplete?

Need a hint?

pd.date_range("2026-11-16 14:00", periods=120, freq="30s") makes the timestamps. Use them as the index, filter out the outage with a boolean mask, then call .resample("5min").agg(["mean", "min", "max", "count"]). A full bucket has 10 readings.

Show solution

The 14:20 bucket is empty, and its NaN mean is the correct answer: there's no data. Plot code that fills NaN with zero would draw a dramatic and fake temperature crash. Always carry the count along with the mean, so a dashboard can grey out or label buckets built from fewer readings.

#Exercise 6: Validate payloads before trusting them

A receiver gets these payload strings. Write validate(text) that returns (True, "ok") or (False, reason). Rules: it must be valid JSON; device is a non-empty string; seq is a positive integer (and not true, which Python treats as the integer 1); temp_c is a number between −40 and 125, or null; light_pct is a number from 0 to 100.

Need a hint?

Wrap json.loads in try/except json.JSONDecodeError. Check type(value) is int rather than isinstance(value, int), because isinstance(True, int) is True. For numbers, accept int or float but still reject bool.

Show solution

The string "22.4" looks fine to a person and would even plot in some tools, but arithmetic on it fails or, worse, concatenates. Rejecting it at the door with a clear reason is far easier to debug than a chart that silently skips it. Module 6 adds one more check to this list: is the sender really who it claims to be?

#Challenge: Merge late and duplicated deliveries

After an outage, a receiver has this record of (seq, arrival_s) pairs. Readings 11 to 25 arrived late in one batch at 80 s, and readings 21 to 25 arrived again at 86 s, because the device didn't get the first reply in time and retried. Reading n was taken at 2 × n seconds. Build the clean series: remove duplicates (keep the first arrival), list missing readings out of 1 to 30, and report the median and maximum delivery delay.

Need a hint?

A dictionary keyed by seq keeps one entry per reading: only store an arrival if the key isn't there yet. The delay for a reading is its arrival time minus 2 * seq.

Show solution

Retries make duplicates unavoidable: a device that never got the confirmation can't know whether the server received the batch, so it sends again. Receivers handle that by making delivery idempotent, meaning that storing the same seq twice has the same effect as storing it once. MQTT, the protocol in Module 5, has quality-of-service levels designed around exactly this problem.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what a broker does and why publishers and subscribers never talk to each other directly.
  • Design a topic tree that says where a reading came from, and send units inside the payload.
  • Predict which topics a + or # subscription receives.
  • Choose QoS 0, 1, or 2 for a message, and use retained messages and a last will for device status.
  • Use public test brokers without leaking anything you care about.

Three Pico W boards publish to a topic called temp. The dashboard receives 21.5, then 70.2, then 22. Is one greenhouse bed at 70 degrees and about to cook the tomatoes, or is one board reporting Fahrenheit? Which bed is the 22? Every number is correct and the dashboard still can't use any of them.

MQTT, the messaging protocol most IoT devices speak, can carry these readings to any number of screens. Naming them so the screens can make sense of them is still your job.

#Why devices talk through a broker

The obvious design has the dashboard ask each device for its reading. It breaks fast: the dashboard needs every device's address, home routers block incoming connections, and a board asleep to save battery can't answer.

MQTT turns this around. Every device opens one outgoing connection to a server called a broker. A device publishes a message to a topic (a name like greenhouse/bed1/temperature). Any client that has subscribed to that topic gets a copy from the broker. The publisher doesn't know who is listening, and the subscribers don't know who published. Either side can come and go.

Notice the logger never received the humidity message. It only asked for temperatures, and the broker filters for it.

Popular brokers include Mosquitto (open source; it runs happily on a Raspberry Pi), HiveMQ, and EMQX. For learning, there are free public brokers at broker.hivemq.com and test.mosquitto.org, both on port 1883, and the Pico W in Wokwi can reach either one.

#Topics are addresses you design

A topic is a UTF-8 string split into levels by /. Topics don't need to be created first: the first publish to a name brings it into existence. That convenience is also the trap, because a typo silently creates a new topic nobody listens to.

Build topics from general to specific, the way a postal address goes country, city, street:

Ambiguous topic Better topic Why
temp c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/bed1/temperature Says where, and leaves room for bed2
greenhouse/temp_F .../bed1/temperature with "unit": "F" in the payload Units belong with the value, not in the name
/greenhouse/bed1 greenhouse/bed1/... A leading / creates an empty first level
Greenhouse/Bed 1/Temp greenhouse/bed1/temperature Topics are case-sensitive; spaces invite typos
.../bed1/2026-11-16T10:02 .../bed1/temperature Never put changing values in a topic; it makes a new topic every time

The random code (a7f3c9 here) matters on a public broker. Everyone in the world shares the same topic space, so a plain greenhouse/bed1/temperature collides with strangers who picked the same name. Make your own code by mashing six random letters and digits, and don't use your name or school.

#Wildcards: subscribe to many topics at once

Subscribers can use two wildcards in a topic filter:

  • + matches exactly one level. c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/+/temperature gets the temperature of every bed.
  • # matches any number of levels, including zero, and must be the last character. c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/# gets everything at the site.

Publishers can't use wildcards; a message always goes to one exact topic. Here is a short matcher that follows the same rules. Step through it and watch how it compares one level at a time and gives up at the first mismatch:

The second call fails at the very end: every level it checked matched, but the topic has four levels and the filter only three. One + never swallows two levels.

#Payloads: say what the number means

The broker treats a payload as raw bytes and never looks inside. That freedom means you decide the format, and JSON is the usual choice because every language can read it. A good reading carries its value, its unit, which device sent it, and a sequence number that goes up by one each time:

Sixty-odd bytes is tiny, even for a Pico. The seq field pays off later: if the dashboard sees 118 and then 120, it knows 119 went missing.

#QoS: how hard the network tries

Wi-Fi drops packets. MQTT lets each message choose a Quality of Service level:

QoS Promise How Good for
0 At most once Send and forget Readings that repeat every few seconds anyway
1 At least once Resend until the receiver answers PUBACK Status changes, alarms, commands; duplicates are possible
2 Exactly once A four-packet handshake (PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP) Rare; when a duplicate would cause harm and the extra traffic is fine

QoS 1 duplicates sound strange until you see why: if the message arrives but the PUBACK is lost on the way back, the sender can't tell the difference and sends again. This simulation pushes 20 messages over a link that loses a quarter of all packets:

QoS 0 lost three readings and nobody noticed. QoS 1 lost none, but three arrived twice, so a subscriber that counts events should use seq to ignore repeats.

Two details trip people up. A subscriber gets the lower of the publisher's and its own QoS, so a QoS 1 publish to a QoS 0 subscription arrives as QoS 0. And umqtt.simple, the library you'll use on the Pico, supports only QoS 0 and 1.

#Retained messages and the last will

Open a dashboard at 10:02 and it shows nothing until the next reading arrives. Worse, it can't tell a quiet station from a dead one. Two MQTT features fix this.

A retained message is one the broker keeps. It stores the last retained message on each topic and hands it to every new subscriber immediately. Retain things that describe current state, like online, or fan: on. To erase a retained message, publish an empty payload to the same topic with the retain flag set.

A last will is a message a client gives the broker when it connects: "if I vanish without saying goodbye, publish this for me." The broker sends it if the connection dies, or if it hears nothing from the client for one and a half times the keepalive interval the client chose. A polite disconnect cancels it.

#Public brokers are postcards

On broker.hivemq.com or test.mosquitto.org there are no passwords. Anyone can subscribe to # and read every message from every user, and anyone can publish to your topics. HiveMQ says its public broker "is not intended for private or production data", and the Mosquitto test server asks: "Please don't publish anything sensitive, anybody could be listening." Wokwi's public Wi-Fi gateway adds a third reader, since Wokwi monitors that traffic for abuse.

So the rules for this course are simple. Use your random code, never your name. Publish sensor numbers, never personal details, locations, or passwords. Never let a public-broker topic switch on anything real. Module 6 deals with the fact that strangers can publish to your topics; for a real project you'd run your own broker, such as Mosquitto on a Raspberry Pi, with accounts and access rules.

⚠️ Watch out

Four bugs that make messages "disappear."

  • Case and spelling. The station publishes to .../greenhouse/... and the dashboard subscribes to .../Greenhouse/#. No error appears anywhere; the subscriber just hears nothing. Copy topic strings, don't retype them.
  • A leading slash. /c4t-lab/... and c4t-lab/... are different topics.
  • # in the middle. c4t-lab/#/temperature is not a valid filter; # must be last. Use + for a single level.
  • Two clients with one client ID. A broker allows one connection per client ID, so when a second one connects, the first is kicked off. If both reconnect automatically they take turns kicking each other off forever. Give every board and every browser tab its own ID.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The dashboard subscribes to c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/+/temperature. Which message does it receive?

  • + matches the single level bed2, and every other level matches exactly.

  • There are two levels (bed2/soil) where the filter has one +. A + never spans levels.

  • This topic has one level fewer than the filter, so the + has nothing to match.

Show answer

A. + matches the single level bed2, and every other level matches exactly.

2A soil sensor sends a reading every 10 seconds, and a missed one doesn't matter. A "frost alarm" message goes out once when the temperature drops below 2 °C. Which QoS levels fit?

  • QoS 2 costs four packets per message. A reading that is replaced in 10 seconds doesn't need that.

  • A lost reading is replaced soon, but a lost alarm is never repeated. QoS 1 might deliver it twice, which is harmless for an alarm.

  • This is backwards: the one-off message is the one that must not be lost.

Show answer

B. A lost reading is replaced soon, but a lost alarm is never repeated. QoS 1 might deliver it twice, which is harmless for an alarm.

3Your station sets a last will of offline with retain on, publishes a retained online, then you press Stop in Wokwi. A dashboard connects five minutes later. What does it see on the status topic?

  • The broker, not the station, delivers retained messages, so the station doesn't need to be there.

  • The station did publish online, but the broker then published the will, which replaced it.

  • The connection died without a goodbye, so the broker published the will. It was retained, so new subscribers get it right away.

Show answer

C. The connection died without a goodbye, so the broker published the will. It was retained, so new subscribers get it right away.

4Which topic is safest to use on broker.hivemq.com?

  • It names a school, a room, and a person, and anyone subscribed to # sees it.

  • The random code avoids collisions and says nothing about who you are.

  • It reveals nothing, but every stranger using the same name will mix their readings with yours.

Show answer

B. The random code avoids collisions and says nothing about who you are.

Key takeaways

  • A broker sits in the middle: devices publish to topics, and the broker copies each message to every subscriber whose filter matches.
  • Design topics from general to specific, keep them lowercase with no leading slash, and put units, device ID, and a sequence number in the payload.
  • + matches one level; # matches everything below and must come last.
  • QoS 0 may lose messages, QoS 1 may duplicate them, QoS 2 does neither at a higher cost.
  • Retain current state, and set a retained last will so silence turns into a clear offline.
  • Public brokers are readable and writable by everyone: random codes, no personal data, nothing that controls real hardware.

#Further reading

  • MQTT Essentials: topics and best practices (HiveMQ) (opens in a new tab): more wildcard examples and naming advice from a broker vendor's long-running tutorial series.
  • MQTT Essentials: last will and testament (HiveMQ) (opens in a new tab): exactly when the broker does and doesn't send the will.
  • MQTT 3.1.1 specification (OASIS) (opens in a new tab): the source of truth. Section 4.7 covers topic names and filters, and it is readable.

What you'll learn

  • Connect a Wokwi Pico W to Wi-Fi and to broker.hivemq.com with umqtt.simple.
  • Publish temperature and humidity as JSON on a topic tree you designed, without blocking the main loop.
  • Announce online with a retained message and let a last will announce offline.
  • Watch the traffic in the HiveMQ web client, then build a dashboard page that flags stale readings.

By the end of this lesson a DHT22 sensor in your browser reports to a real broker on the internet, and a web page on your computer shows the numbers with their age. When you stop the simulation, the page notices.

Here is what the HiveMQ web client will show once it works (the topic, then the payload):

#Step 1: Write down the topic plan

Decide the names before writing code, so the station and the dashboard agree. Replace a7f3c9 with your own random code everywhere in this lesson.

Topic Payload Retained? QoS
c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/bed1/temperature {"v": 24.0, "unit": "C", "dev": "station-01", "seq": 1} No 0
c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/bed1/humidity {"v": 40.0, "unit": "%", "dev": "station-01", "seq": 1} No 0
c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/devices/station-01/status online or offline Yes 1

Readings repeat every five seconds, so a lost one costs nothing and they aren't retained. Status is current state that a late subscriber needs, so it is retained and sent with QoS 1.

#Step 2: Set up the Wokwi project

  1. Open the Pico W MicroPython template (opens in a new tab). It starts with a main.py that prints a greeting.
  2. Click the + button above the diagram, search for DHT22, and drop it next to the board.
  3. Wire it by clicking a pin and then its partner:
DHT22 pin Pico W pin
VCC 3V3
SDA GP15
NC (leave empty)
GND any GND

The official Pico W firmware doesn't include it, so open the umqtt.simple source (opens in a new tab), copy all of it, create a new file in your Wokwi project (from the arrow menu at the end of the file tabs), name it umqttsimple.py, and paste. Wokwi copies every project file onto the simulated board's flash, so main.py can import it.

💡 Tip

Wokwi's own documentation describes Wi-Fi for its Pico 2 W board. If your Pico W project never gets past Joining Wi-Fi...., start again from the Pico 2 W MicroPython template (opens in a new tab) and copy your files across; every line of code in this module runs unchanged on it.

📝 Note

On a real Pico W, install the library instead: in Thonny use Tools › Manage packages and search for micropython-umqtt.simple, or run import mip; mip.install("umqtt.simple") once the board is on Wi-Fi. Then write from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient wherever this lesson writes from umqttsimple import MQTTClient.

#Step 3: Join Wi-Fi and connect with a last will

Replace main.py with this and press the green play button.

Three decisions hide in those last four lines. The client ID includes your code, because two clients with the same ID knock each other off the broker. set_last_will must come before connect(), since the will travels inside the CONNECT packet. And keepalive=30 tells the broker to expect a sign of life at least every 30 seconds; without it, umqtt.simple asks for no keepalive at all, and the broker might wait a very long time before deciding the station is gone.

If you see OSError after Joining Wi-Fi, the simulator's internet gateway is busy; stop and start the simulation again. An ImportError for umqttsimple means the file name in Step 2 doesn't match exactly.

#Step 4: Publish readings without blocking

A station that calls time.sleep(5) between readings can't do anything else for those five seconds, and in Module 6 it must also listen for commands. So the loop wakes every 50 ms and checks whether a reading is due, using ticks_ms() and ticks_diff(), which handle the millisecond counter wrapping around.

A failed sensor read prints a message and skips the publish rather than sending a made-up value. A dashboard that shows nothing is honest; one that shows a stale number as if it were fresh is not.

#Step 5: Watch the traffic in the HiveMQ web client

  1. Open the HiveMQ web client (opens in a new tab) in a new tab. Leave Host and Port as they are and click Connect.
  2. Click Add New Topic Subscription, type c4t-lab/a7f3c9/# (with your code), and click Subscribe.
  3. The Messages panel fills up every five seconds. The status message arrives first, straight away, because it is retained.

Now test each feature on purpose:

  • Change the world. Click the DHT22 in Wokwi and drag its temperature slider. The next message carries the new value.
  • Test the retained message. Disconnect the web client, connect again, and resubscribe. online appears instantly; readings only arrive on the next publish.
  • Test the last will. Stop the Wokwi simulation. Within about 45 seconds (one and a half keepalive periods), sometimes sooner, offline arrives on the status topic. Start the simulation again and it flips back to online.

#Step 6: Build a dashboard that knows when data is stale

The web client is a debugging tool. A dashboard should show the latest value per sensor and how old it is. The rule here: a tile turns stale after 15 seconds without news, which means three missed readings in a row.

The preview below runs the dashboard code with a demo feed standing in for the broker: bed2's station stops after 20 seconds and station-01 goes offline after 45. Watch the tiles change.

Look at how show() treats its input. Anyone on the internet can publish to your topics on a public broker, so the dashboard assumes every payload might be junk or an attack. It ignores anything that isn't valid JSON with a numeric v and a known unit, and it writes text with textContent, never innerHTML. With innerHTML, a stranger could publish <img src=x onerror=...> as a "unit" and run their own script in your page.

Save it and double-click it to open it in your browser while the Wokwi simulation runs. Browsers can't open raw MQTT connections, so the page uses MQTT over secure WebSockets on port 8884, which the HiveMQ broker also offers. The random client ID means two open tabs don't fight.

#The finished station

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is the status topic retained while the readings are not?

  • Retain current state. A retained reading would show a new dashboard an old number with no hint of its age, unless the payload carried a trustworthy timestamp.

  • Retain and QoS are independent flags; any QoS can be retained.

  • The broker never looks inside payloads, so it can retain anything.

Show answer

A. Retain current state. A retained reading would show a new dashboard an old number with no hint of its age, unless the payload carried a trustworthy timestamp.

2Someone publishes {"v": 5, "unit": "<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>"} to your temperature topic. What does the dashboard do?

  • That would happen with innerHTML. The dashboard never builds HTML from payloads.

  • The UNITS check rejects it before anything is drawn, and even an accepted value is written with textContent, which displays characters instead of running them.

  • The payload is valid JSON; the problem is what's inside it, which is why the checks after parsing matter.

Show answer

B. The UNITS check rejects it before anything is drawn, and even an accepted value is written with textContent, which displays characters instead of running them.

3You open dashboard.html in two tabs. What happens, and why?

  • That would happen with a fixed client ID. Each tab makes a random one, so both stay connected.

  • Each tab is a separate subscriber with its own client ID, and the broker sends each one a copy.

Show answer

B. Each tab is a separate subscriber with its own client ID, and the broker sends each one a copy.

Key takeaways

  • Write the topic plan first; both the station and the dashboard depend on it.
  • Call set_last_will before connect(), set a keepalive, and give every client a unique ID.
  • A loop that checks ticks_diff every few milliseconds publishes on schedule and stays free for other work.

What you'll learn

  • Turn ambiguous topics into a plan that names place, measurement, and unit.
  • Check topic filters against MQTT's wildcard rules and route messages to subscribers.
  • Reject payloads that a dashboard shouldn't trust.
  • Use sequence numbers to spot lost, repeated, and restarted streams.
  • Chart readings and mark which ones have gone stale.

#Warm-up: who hears this message?

A station publishes to c4t-lab/q8z2rw/greenhouse/bed2/humidity. Without running anything, decide which of these subscriptions receive it:

  1. c4t-lab/q8z2rw/#
  2. c4t-lab/+/greenhouse/+/humidity
  3. c4t-lab/q8z2rw/greenhouse/+
  4. #
  5. c4t-lab/q8z2rw/greenhouse/bed2/humidity/#
Show solution

1, 2, 4, and 5 receive it. Number 3 fails because + covers one level and the topic has two left (bed2/humidity). Number 5 surprises people: # also matches zero levels, so x/# receives messages on x itself.

#Exercise 1: Untangle a messy topic scheme

A previous student's greenhouse sent these messages. Write a new topic and payload for each, using the prefix c4t-lab/q8z2rw/greenhouse.

Old topic Old payload What it really was
temp 72 Bed 1 air temperature, Fahrenheit
temp 22.5 Bed 2 air temperature, Celsius
hum 0.41 Bed 1 humidity as a fraction
greenhouseTemp 23 Bed 2 again, from a second board
/Bed 2/Soil 310 Bed 2 soil moisture, raw ADC count
status 1 Station 1 is running
Need a hint?

One topic per measurement per place. Units go in the payload, and you can convert a fraction to a percentage before publishing. A raw ADC count is a legitimate unit if you say so.

Show solution
New topic New payload
.../bed1/temperature {"v": 72, "unit": "F", "dev": "station-01", "seq": 1}
.../bed2/temperature {"v": 22.5, "unit": "C", "dev": "station-02", "seq": 1}
.../bed1/humidity {"v": 41, "unit": "%", "dev": "station-01", "seq": 1}
.../bed2/temperature {"v": 23, "unit": "C", "dev": "station-03", "seq": 1}
.../bed2/soil {"v": 310, "unit": "adc", "dev": "station-02", "seq": 1}
.../devices/station-01/status online (retained, with offline as the last will)

Two boards now publish to bed2/temperature, and that is fine, because dev tells them apart. If you want them on separate tiles, add a level: bed2/temperature/station-03. The fractional humidity became a percentage so every humidity reading in the system means the same thing.

#Exercise 2: Validate a topic filter

Write valid_filter(f) that returns False for filters a broker would reject. The rules: a filter can't be empty, # must be a whole level on its own and the last level, and + must be a whole level on its own. Empty levels (a//b) are allowed.

Need a hint?

Split on / and use enumerate so you know when you're at the last level. For each level, ask: does it contain a wildcard character, and if so, is the level exactly that character?

Show solution

"#" in level catches bed#, and the i != len(levels) - 1 part catches a # that is a whole level but not the last one.

#Exercise 3: Route messages, and keep $SYS private

Brokers publish their own statistics on topics that start with $, such as $SYS/broker/uptime. The MQTT rule: a filter that starts with a wildcard never matches a topic that starts with $, so a # subscriber doesn't drown in broker internals. Add that rule to the matcher from the notes, then write route() so it prints who receives each message.

Need a hint?

The $ check goes at the top of matches(), before any splitting: look at the topic's first character and the filter's first character. In route(), a list comprehension over subscriptions.items() collects the names.

Show solution

Look at the snoop column: a # subscriber receives every other student's messages too. That is what "public broker" means in practice.

#Exercise 4: Reject payloads you shouldn't trust

Write parse_reading(topic, payload) for a dashboard. It returns a clean dict, converting Fahrenheit to Celsius, or a string saying why the message was rejected. It must survive everything in this inbox:

Need a hint?

json.loads raises ValueError on bad JSON, and json.loads(b"23.4") happily returns a float, so check that you got a dict. Watch out for true: in Python, isinstance(True, int) is True, so test for bool first.

Show solution

The string "41" is rejected on purpose. Quietly converting it would hide a bug in whichever station sent it.

#Exercise 5: Find lost, repeated, and restarted messages

A dashboard logged these seq values from one station: [1, 2, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6, 7, 10, 1, 2, 3]. Write audit(seqs) that reports which numbers were lost, which arrived twice (QoS 1 at work), and when the station restarted its count.

Need a hint?

Keep the last number you accepted. A jump from last to s loses range(last + 1, s). A value you've already seen in this run is a duplicate. A 1 after a bigger number means the count started over, so reset what you remember.

Show solution

The restart check matters more than it looks. Without it, the second 1, 2, 3 would be flagged as duplicates, and in Module 6 the same mistake, made in the other direction, lets an attacker replay old commands after a reboot.

#Exercise 6: A chart dashboard that shows staleness

Here is a log of messages: bed1 reports every 5 seconds in Celsius, and bed2 reports in Fahrenheit until t = 40 s and then goes silent. At t = 75 s, print each bed's latest value in Celsius, its age, and whether it is stale (older than 15 s). Then chart both beds and shade the period where bed2 was stale.

Need a hint?

Group readings per bed into lists of (t, celsius) pairs with dict.setdefault. The latest reading is the last pair. A bed becomes stale 15 s after its last message, so the shading runs from last_t + 15 to now; plt.axvspan draws a shaded band.

Show solution

Converting bed2 to Celsius before plotting is what makes the two lines comparable. Plotted raw, bed2 would sit near 72 and look like a heat wave.

#Challenge: Build a broker that retains and keeps wills

Write a MiniBroker class that stores retained messages, sends them to new subscribers, keeps each client's last will, and publishes the will only when a client vanishes without a clean disconnect. Use any matcher from this lesson. Until your class exists, this test script stops with an error; once the class works, it must print the output below it:

Four dictionaries or lists cover the state: subscriptions as (client, filter) pairs, retained as topic to payload, wills as client to (topic, payload, retain), and an inbox per client. On subscribe, loop over retained and deliver matches. On an unclean disconnect, call your own publish with the will.

Show solution

late never saw 23.4: it wasn't retained, so it vanished the moment it was delivered. It did see offline, because the will was published with retain on and replaced online. wills.pop on a clean disconnect is what keeps spare's will from firing.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a secret-looking topic name protects nothing.
  • Tell identity, authentication, and authorization apart, and say which part a password, a TLS certificate, or an access list handles.
  • Describe in plain words what TLS gives a device, and what it does not.
  • Sign and verify a command with HMAC-SHA256, and explain why a plain hash can't do the job.
  • Recognize a replay attack and block it with a timestamp window, a nonce, or a counter.

Your greenhouse station is about to get a fan it can switch on when the air gets hot. The obvious design: the station subscribes to c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/bed1/fan/set, and when a message saying on arrives, it turns the fan on.

Here is what a stranger subscribed to # on the public broker sees a few minutes after you test it:

They don't need to guess anything. They can publish on at 3 a.m., or every half second, and your station obeys. A random code in the topic stops accidental collisions, but it isn't a secret, because every message carries it in plain view.

#Identity, authentication, authorization

These three words sound alike and answer different questions.

Question Name Greenhouse example
Who do you say you are? Identity Client ID station-01, or the board's machine.unique_id()
Can you prove it? Authentication A password, a secret key, or a certificate's private key
What are you allowed to do? Authorization station-01 may publish readings; only the controller may publish to fan/set

An identity on its own is just a claim. Anyone can connect with the client ID station-01, and a chip's unique ID is printed in plain sight by the first line of code that reads it. Authentication needs something only the real device knows.

A private broker, such as Mosquitto on a Raspberry Pi, can do the first two jobs itself: each device logs in with a username and password, and an access control list (ACL) says which topics each username can read or write. A Mosquitto ACL file looks like this:

With allow_anonymous false and a password file in its configuration, that broker simply refuses a stranger's publish to fan/set. The public brokers you're using can't do any of this, which is why this module also protects each message on its own.

#TLS in plain words

A username and password sent over a plain MQTT connection (port 1883) travel as readable text. Everyone on the path can read them: the Wi-Fi network, the internet provider, and in this course Wokwi's public gateway too.

TLS (the same technology as the padlock in your browser) wraps the connection in three protections:

  1. Encryption. An eavesdropper sees scrambled bytes instead of your password and readings.
  2. Server authentication. The broker shows a certificate signed by an authority your device already trusts. A fake broker can't produce one for your broker's name, so the device knows it reached the real thing.
  3. Integrity. Change a single byte in transit and the receiver notices and drops the connection.

MQTT over TLS normally uses port 8883, and MQTT over secure WebSockets (what your dashboard uses) port 8884 on HiveMQ's broker. On a real Pico W with a private broker, the connection looks something like this:

The two comments carry the lessons. MicroPython's documentation warns that CERT_REQUIRED needs the device's date and time set properly. And with CERT_NONE, the connection is encrypted but the Pico never checks the certificate, so it would happily send its password to an impostor.

Notice what TLS does not do. It protects the pipe between one client and the broker. On a public broker, a stranger opens their own perfectly valid TLS connection and publishes to your topic. TLS can't tell you whether a message came from someone you trust; only a key you share with your controller can.

#Why a plain hash isn't a signature

A hash function like SHA-256 turns any message into a 64-character fingerprint, and changing one character changes the whole fingerprint. That makes it tempting to send a command along with its hash. Try it:

A hash catches accidents, like a corrupted byte. It does nothing against an attacker, because the attacker can run SHA-256 too.

#HMAC: a tag only key holders can make

The fix is to mix a secret key into the hash. HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) does that in a careful, standard way: HMAC-SHA256(key, message) gives a 32-byte tag. Anyone can see the message and the tag, but making a valid tag for a new message requires the key. The controller and the station share the key; nobody else has it.

To verify, the station recomputes the tag from the message it received and its own copy of the key, then compares.

Three details in that code matter:

  • What gets signed is a string built from the fields in a fixed order, joined with |. Signing JSON text is fragile: JSON with different spacing or key order means the same thing but produces a different tag, and MicroPython dictionaries don't even keep keys in order. Both sides build the same string from the same fields.
  • Every field the device acts on is signed, including the device name. Leave a field out of the signed string and an attacker can change it freely.
  • hmac.compare_digest takes the same time whether the first character differs or the last. A normal == stops at the first mismatch, and with enough attempts an attacker can time those tiny differences to discover a valid tag one character at a time.

#Replay attacks: a valid message, used twice

HMAC proves a message came from a key holder. It says nothing about when. An attacker who records your genuine, correctly signed fan_on can publish an exact copy of it tonight, tomorrow, or a thousand times, and every copy passes the signature check.

The defense is to sign something that makes each message usable only once:

  • A counter. Each command carries a number one higher than the last. The station remembers the highest number it accepted and rejects anything not above it. No clock needed, but the station must remember the number even after it reboots.
  • A timestamp window. Each command carries the time it was made, and the station rejects anything older than, say, 30 seconds. This needs the two clocks to agree, which is harder than it sounds: a Wokwi simulation can run slower than real time, so the board's clock drifts.
  • A nonce ("number used once"). Each command carries a random value, and the station remembers the values it has seen. Pair it with a timestamp so the station only has to remember nonces from inside the window.

Here is a timestamp plus a nonce, tested against four attacks:

Read the results as a list of attacks that failed. A quick replay hits the nonce check. A late replay hits the time window. Editing ts to look fresh breaks the signature, because ts is part of the signed string. And a command signed for station-01 doesn't work on station-02, even though both happen to share this demo key.

⚠️ Watch out

Signed, but still unsafe. Four mistakes show up again and again in student projects:

  • Acting before checking. led.on() placed above the signature check runs for every message. Verify first, act second.
  • Signing part of the message. If the tag covers fan_on|7 but the device also reads a duration field, an attacker can change the duration to 10 hours without breaking the tag.
  • Comparing tags with ==. Use hmac.compare_digest in Python, or the loop you'll write for MicroPython.
  • Putting the key where it travels. A key printed to the console, published in an error message, or pasted into a public Wokwi project is no longer a secret. Module 7 is about where keys should live.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Your station checks that the client ID in a command's payload is controller before acting. What does this stop?

  • There is no key involved: the client ID is a claim, and anyone can type controller.

  • Identity says who someone claims to be. Without a secret to prove it, any stranger can make the same claim.

  • A replayed message carries the same client ID as the original, so this check passes it straight through.

Show answer

B. Identity says who someone claims to be. Without a secret to prove it, any stranger can make the same claim.

2The broker connection uses TLS with certificate checking on. Which attack is still possible on a public broker?

  • That is exactly what TLS encryption prevents.

  • Certificate checking stops impostor brokers, as long as verify_mode is CERT_REQUIRED.

  • TLS protects each client's pipe to the broker, not who is allowed to publish. That needs broker ACLs or signed messages.

Show answer

C. TLS protects each client's pipe to the broker, not who is allowed to publish. That needs broker ACLs or signed messages.

3A command's tag is HMAC(key, "fan_on"), and the payload is {"cmd": "fan_on", "minutes": 5, "sig": ...}. What can an attacker who records it do?

  • The tag only covers the text fan_on, so everything else in the payload is unprotected.

  • The tag doesn't cover minutes, and nothing in it makes the message one-use. Sign every field the device uses, plus a counter or a timestamp and nonce.

  • HMAC-SHA256 is designed so that seeing tags, even many of them, doesn't reveal the key.

Show answer

B. The tag doesn't cover minutes, and nothing in it makes the message one-use. Sign every field the device uses, plus a counter or a timestamp and nonce.

4A Wokwi station uses a 30-second timestamp window. After an hour of simulation, every genuine command is rejected as too old. What is the most likely cause?

  • A wrong key would give "bad signature", not "too old".

  • The station's clock and the controller's clock disagree by more than the window. A counter avoids depending on clocks at all.

  • The cache only rejects repeated nonces, and each genuine command has a new one.

Show answer

B. The station's clock and the controller's clock disagree by more than the window. A counter avoids depending on clocks at all.

Key takeaways

  • Topic names are public. Anyone on a public broker can read them and publish to them.
  • Identity is a claim, authentication is proof, authorization is a list of what each proven identity may do.
  • TLS gives encryption, a verified broker, and tamper detection on the connection; it needs certificate checking on and a correct clock, and it doesn't decide who may publish.
  • HMAC-SHA256 with a shared key gives a tag only key holders can create. Sign a fixed-order string of every field the device acts on, and compare with compare_digest.
  • A valid signature can be replayed. Add a counter, or a timestamp plus a nonce, inside the signed string.

#Further reading

  • Python hmac module (opens in a new tab): hmac.new, hexdigest, and the note on why compare_digest exists.
  • MQTT security fundamentals: TLS (HiveMQ) (opens in a new tab): how TLS fits MQTT, including the cost on small devices.
  • OWASP Internet of Things Project (opens in a new tab): the IoT Top 10 list of the most common device security failures, several of which you can now name.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Generate a shared key and sign commands with a small Python tool.
  • Implement HMAC-SHA256 with only hashlib, and prove it matches Python's hmac module.
  • Write one checking function that rejects bad JSON, bad signatures, wrong devices, unknown commands, and replayed sequence numbers.
  • Subscribe the Pico W to a command topic, drive a "fan" LED, and publish the result to a retained state topic and an audit log.

The station from Module 5 gets a fan (an LED on GP16 stands in for it). By the end, the fan obeys exactly one kind of message: a command signed with your key, addressed to station-01, naming a known command, with a sequence number it hasn't seen. Everything else is refused and written to an audit topic, so you can see who tried what.

We use a counter for replay protection rather than a timestamp, because the simulated board's clock can drift away from your computer's. Each command's seq must be higher than the last one the station accepted.

#Step 1: Make a key and a signing tool

On your own computer, make a random key:

That prints 64 hex characters, which is 256 bits of randomness. You'll use those 64 characters as the key bytes on both sides. This key protects a simulated LED, so treat it as a throwaway; Module 7 is about handling keys that protect something real.

The signing tool runs on your computer with nothing but the standard library. It builds the signed string device|command|seq in a fixed order and prints a JSON command ready to paste:

Copy the last line of your own output; that is the whole command. The signature is the only part that needs the key, so the JSON itself can be read by anyone without harm.

#Step 2: HMAC for a board without an hmac module

MicroPython on the Pico has hashlib.sha256 but no hmac. Fortunately HMAC is short enough to write yourself, straight from its definition (RFC 2104):

  1. Pad the key with zero bytes to SHA-256's block size, 64 bytes. (A longer key is hashed first.)
  2. Make two keys from it: every byte XOR 0x36 (the inner key) and every byte XOR 0x5C (the outer key).
  3. tag = SHA256(outer_key + SHA256(inner_key + message)).

Never trust a hand-written crypto function until it matches a known-good one, so this cell checks it against Python's hmac on keys that are exactly 64 bytes, short, long, and empty:

All four match, and the first tag starts with the same characters as the signature from Step 1. binascii.hexlify replaces .hexdigest(), which MicroPython's hashlib doesn't have. And same() is MicroPython's stand-in for hmac.compare_digest: it always walks the whole string, folding every difference into diff, so it takes the same time wherever the first mismatch is.

#Step 3: One function that decides

All the rules live in check_command. It runs unchanged on your computer and on the Pico, so you can attack it here, with ten messages, before it ever touches hardware. The order matters: parse, check types, verify the signature, and only then look at what the message asks for.

Only the two genuine, fresh commands get through. The "unknown cmd" row is worth a second look: it was signed with the real key, so it came from you, and the station still refuses it. An allowlist protects you from your own controller's bugs, too.

#Step 4: Wire the fan and save the counter

Add an LED to the Wokwi diagram with the + button, plus a resistor (set it to 220 Ω):

From To
GP16 resistor, one end
resistor, other end LED anode (A, the bent leg)
LED cathode (C) GND

Then add two files to the project next to umqttsimple.py:

  • hmac_lite.py: the three functions from Step 2 (hmac_sha256, hmac_sha256_hex, same) plus import binascii and import hashlib at the top.
  • secrets.py: one line holding the same key as your signing tool:

The station must remember last_seq across reboots, or a restart would accept every old command again. It saves the number to a small file each time it accepts a command:

On a real Pico W that file lives in flash and survives power cuts. In Wokwi, files your program writes don't survive a restart: each run starts from a fresh copy of the project files, so the counter goes back to 0 when you press Stop and Play. Keep that in mind when testing; the practice lesson has you fix it.

#Step 5: Subscribe, check, act, and log

Here is the complete station. Compared with Module 5 it adds the fan pin, a callback that runs check_command, a subscribe call, and client.check_msg() in the loop, which handles any waiting message and returns at once if there is none.

A few lines deserve a closer look:

  • set_callback must come before subscribe; umqtt.simple refuses to subscribe without one. And client is made global inside connect_broker because a message can arrive while subscribe() is still waiting for the broker's reply, and on_message publishes through client.
  • The audit entry for a rejection records the reason only. It never echoes the payload, so a stranger can't use your audit topic to bounce their own text around, and it never contains the key.
  • The fan state is published retained with its seq, so a dashboard sees whether the fan is on, and you can see which number to sign next.

#Step 6: Attack your own fan

Run the simulation, open the HiveMQ web client, connect, and subscribe to c4t-lab/a7f3c9/# so you see the audit topic. Then use its Publish box with the topic c4t-lab/a7f3c9/greenhouse/bed1/fan/set, and leave Retain unchecked:

  1. Paste the signed fan_on command with seq 1 and click Publish. The LED lights, and the audit topic shows accepted.
  2. Click Publish again without changing anything. That's a replay. The audit shows replayed or old seq and nothing changes.
  3. Change fan_on to fan_off in the message box but keep the old sig. Result: bad signature.
  4. Publish the word on. Result: not JSON.
  5. Run sign_command.py again for fan_off with seq 2 and publish it. The LED goes dark.

(The dictionary keys may print in another order on the Pico.)

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does check_command verify the signature before checking seq <= last_seq?

  • A message is untrusted until its tag checks out. Checking the signature first means every later decision is about a message you actually sent.

  • Comparing two integers is far cheaper than an HMAC; speed isn't the reason.

  • Maybe, but the order is about trust, not frequency.

Show answer

A. A message is untrusted until its tag checks out. Checking the signature first means every later decision is about a message you actually sent.

2The station accepts seq 5. You then sign fan_on with seq 4 by mistake. What happens, and why is that the right behavior?

  • A valid signature proves you sent it, not that it's new. An old genuine message is exactly what a replay looks like.

  • Any number at or below the last accepted one is refused, whoever sent it. Sign with 6 instead.

  • The counter only moves up, and only after a fully valid command.

Show answer

B. Any number at or below the last accepted one is refused, whoever sent it. Sign with 6 instead.

3Why does the station save last_seq to a file?

  • Writing to flash is slower than keeping a variable; the file is about memory across restarts.

  • If last_seq restarted at 0, an attacker could replay your seq 1 command after any power cut. In Wokwi the file resets on every start, which is a simulator limit to remember.

Show answer

B. If last_seq restarted at 0, an attacker could replay your seq 1 command after any power cut. In Wokwi the file resets on every start, which is a simulator limit to remember.

Key takeaways

  • Sign a fixed-order string of every field the device acts on: here device|command|seq.
  • HMAC-SHA256 is two SHA-256 calls with padded, XOR-ed keys; test any hand-written version against a trusted library.
  • Check in this order: parse, types, signature, then device, allowlist, and freshness. Act only after every check passes.
  • A counter needs no clock, but the device must store it somewhere that survives a reboot.
  • Log every decision to an audit topic, with reasons, never the key or the raw rejected payload.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Give each device its own key, so a key pulled out of one stolen board can't command the others.
  • Replace the counter with a timestamp and nonce: call ntptime.settime() after Wi-Fi connects and allow a generous window to absorb simulator drift.
  • Lock out commands for a minute after five bad signatures in a row, and publish a locked audit entry.
  • Write a desktop controller that publishes the signed command itself with the paho-mqtt package, and reads the retained fan/state to pick the next seq automatically.

#Further reading

  • RFC 2104: HMAC (opens in a new tab): the original definition, short and readable. Section 2 is the algorithm you implemented.
  • MicroPython hashlib (opens in a new tab): which hash functions the board offers and why hexdigest() is missing.
  • Python secrets module (opens in a new tab): the right way to make keys, tokens, and nonces on a computer.

What you'll learn

  • Find and fix the ordering, comparison, and coverage bugs in a command handler.
  • Explain why fields must be separated and validated before signing.
  • Keep a replay guard's memory bounded without opening a replay hole.
  • Recover a replay counter after a reboot from a signed, retained message.

#Warm-up: which check stops it?

Match each attack to the check in Lesson 2's check_command that rejects it: types, signature, device, allowlist, or seq.

  1. Publishing the word on.
  2. Resending yesterday's genuine fan_on exactly as it was.
  3. Taking a genuine command and changing "seq": 4 to "seq": 40.
  4. A genuine command you signed for station-02, delivered to station-01.
  5. {"dev": "station-01", "cmd": "fan_on", "seq": "5", "sig": "..."}
Show solution
  1. Types, or really one step earlier: "on" isn't JSON at all.
  2. Seq. The signature is genuine, so only freshness can catch it.
  3. Signature. seq is part of the signed text, so changing it breaks the tag.
  4. Device. The tag is valid, because both boards share the demo key, but the name doesn't match.
  5. Types. "5" is a string, not an integer, so it is refused before any HMAC is computed.

#Exercise 1: Fix a handler that "works"

This handler passes its one happy-path test. Run it against the attacks below and list every problem you see in the output. Then rewrite handle() so that a replay, a forgery, and a command for another board are all rejected, and the fan only changes after every check passes.

Need a hint?

Read the "fan on" column, not just accepted or rejected. The forgery was rejected, and yet the fan changed. Then ask: which fields does the tag cover? Is seq ever compared with anything? Is == the right way to compare tags?

Show solution

Five problems: the fan changes before any check; the tag covers only cmd, so dev and seq can be anything; seq is stored but never compared, so replays pass; there's no device check; and == leaks timing. The fix signs all three fields, checks shape and types, compares with compare_digest, enforces seq, and acts last:

Here the device check runs before the signature check. That's fine because it doesn't change anything; what matters is that nothing acts until the signature has been verified.

#Exercise 2: Two messages, one signature

A student signs a command by gluing its fields together with no separator: cmd + minutes + seq. Show that a signed ("fan_on", 5, 12) also verifies ("fan_on", 51, 2). Then write tag_fixed(*fields) that joins with | and refuses any field that contains a |.

Need a hint?

Both tuples turn into the same string, fan_on512, and HMAC only ever sees the string. A separator restores the boundaries, but only if no field can contain the separator itself.

Show solution

The forged version runs the fan for 51 minutes instead of 5. The counter check might happen to catch this one (2 is lower than 12), but you shouldn't rely on luck: the signed text must have exactly one meaning.

#Exercise 3: A nonce cache that can't be flooded

The timestamp-plus-nonce guard from the notes keeps every nonce from the last 30 seconds. An attacker can't forge nonces, but a buggy controller (or your own script stuck in a loop) could send thousands per second, and a Pico W has only a few hundred kilobytes of RAM in total. Write NonceGuard(window_s=30, max_size=100) whose memory never exceeds max_size, without ever accepting a replay.

Need a hint?

When the cache is full, the tempting move is to throw away the oldest nonce. Don't: that nonce is still inside the window, so its message could be replayed straight away. Refuse the new message instead ("fail closed"), and let time empty the cache.

Show solution

At t=1031 every stored nonce has aged out, so memory drops back to one entry. A nonce that has aged out can't be replayed anyway, because the time check rejects it first.

#Exercise 4: Survive a reboot without reopening replays

In Wokwi, fan_seq.txt resets on every start, so last_seq goes back to 0 and your old seq 1 command works again. One fix uses the broker's memory: the station already publishes a retained fan/state with the last seq. On boot, it can read that back.

But anyone can publish a retained message to that topic. So the station must sign its own state message, and verify it on boot. Write state_message(state, seq) and recover_seq(file_seq, retained), which returns the larger of the file's number and a verified retained number.

Need a hint?

Put a word like state into the signed text, so it reads station-01|state|on|7. Without it, the station's state message for seq 7 could be signed over the very same text as a command, and an attacker could replay your station's own state message as a command.

Show solution

max() means a forgery can never move the counter down. The last line shows the limit of this fix: on a public broker anyone can erase a retained message by publishing an empty one, and then a Wokwi station falls back to 0. A real Pico's flash file, or a private broker whose ACL stops strangers writing to fan/state, closes that gap.

#Exercise 5: Access rules a broker could enforce

On a private broker, the cleanest protection is to stop strangers publishing at all. Write the rules as data and an allowed(user, action, topic) function that denies anything not listed. The station may publish its own readings and status, may read its fan topic, and must not be able to publish to its own fan/set.

Need a hint?

greenhouse/bed1/+ matches bed1/temperature but not bed1/fan/set, which has two levels after bed1. Picking + instead of # is the whole trick for the second line. An unknown user gets an empty rule list, so the default return False covers strangers.

Show solution

In Mosquitto the same rules go in the ACL file as user station-01 followed by topic write greenhouse/bed1/+, and so on. Deny-by-default is what makes it safe: forgetting a rule breaks a feature, which you'll notice, instead of opening a hole, which you won't.

#Exercise 6: Read the audit log

Here is a station's audit log as (seconds, result, detail). Count the rejections by reason, most common first, and print an alert for the first time five bad signatures land within 60 seconds.

Need a hint?

For the alert, collect the times of bad signatures in order. If the 1st and 5th of any run of five are at most 60 seconds apart, that's your window: compare times[i] with times[i + 4].

Show solution

The two not JSON entries a second apart look like a person typing in the web client. Six bad signatures in 50 seconds look like a script. Two replays right after each other at t=2400 suggest someone resending a message they recorded.

#Challenge: Should the station lock itself?

A common instinct is to lock out all commands for two minutes after five bad signatures in a minute. Build that Lockout class, then play the attacker: send five junk messages, then try your own genuine command at t=30, and again at t=150 after the attacker repeats the trick. Decide whether the lockout helps, and what you'd do instead.

Need a hint?

Think about what the lockout protects against. Guessing a 256-bit key one message at a time would take longer than the age of the universe, even with no lockout at all. Now think about what it hands the attacker: five junk messages, which anyone on a public broker can send, switch off your control for two minutes, and they can repeat it forever.

Show solution

The lockout turns a harmless nuisance into a working denial-of-service attack: the attacker never needs the key to stop you controlling your own fan. Lockouts make sense for short secrets such as a 4-digit PIN, where guessing is realistic. With a long random key, a better design keeps accepting genuine commands, publishes an alert like Exercise 6's, and leaves blocking strangers to a broker with accounts and ACLs, where the attacker can't publish in the first place.
