What you'll learn

  • Name the places a password or key leaks from, including some that aren't code.
  • Split configuration from code with secrets.py, secrets.example.py, and .gitignore, and know what to do when a secret was already committed.
  • Rotate a key without downtime using key IDs and a small keyring.
  • Draw a system diagram that shows trust boundaries, and fill in a failure-mode table for it.
  • Reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and explain why retrying instantly makes outages worse.

You push the greenhouse project to GitHub to show a friend. Line 9 of main.py reads WIFI_PASSWORD = "maple-tree-42", and that is your family's Wi-Fi. You notice, delete the line, and push again. It doesn't help. Anyone who clones the repository can run git log -p and read every version of every file, including the one with the password.

This lesson has two halves that belong together: where secrets should live, and how the system behaves when things break. Both are about deciding in advance instead of finding out later.

#Where secrets leak from

A secret is anything that grants access: a Wi-Fi password, a broker password, an HMAC key, an API token. They escape through more doors than people expect:

Leak How it happens Prevention
Source code KEY = b"..." in main.py, then the file is shared or pushed Keep secrets in a separate file that never gets shared
Git history The secret was committed once, then deleted Rotate the secret; deleting it doesn't remove it from history
A public Wokwi project Wokwi's free plan makes saved projects visible to everyone Use throwaway keys in the simulator, never real passwords
Screenshots and screen recordings The editor is open on the secrets file Close it before you share your screen
Logs and audit messages print(config) or an error message that includes the key Log reasons and IDs, never secret values
The device itself The Pico W has no locked storage, so anyone holding the board can copy every file off it over USB One key per device, so a stolen board unlocks only itself

The last row matters for IoT in particular. A web server lives in a locked room; your station sits in a greenhouse anyone can walk into.

#Split code from configuration

The standard fix is three files. The code imports its secrets; the secrets file stays on your machine and on the device; and an example file with fake values shows others what to fill in.

The try block turns a confusing traceback into instructions. Add .gitignore before your first commit; git ignores a file only while it isn't already being tracked.

If a secret was committed anyway, three steps, in this order: change the secret (a new Wi-Fi password, a new key) so the leaked one is worthless; stop tracking the file with git rm --cached secrets.py and commit; then add it to .gitignore. Rewriting history with a tool like git filter-repo is optional cleanup. Rotation is the actual fix, because you can never be sure who already cloned the old version.

⚠️ Watch out

secrets.py on a Raspberry Pi breaks Python's own secrets module. MicroPython has no module called secrets, so the name is safe on the Pico. Regular Python does, and a file with that name in your project folder is found first. Here is what happens to a script on a Pi that tries to make a key:

On a Pi or laptop, call the file device_secrets.py instead, or keep secrets out of the project folder completely: environment variables (os.environ["BROKER_PASSWORD"]) or a config file in your home folder that only your user can read (chmod 600).

#Rotate keys without breaking the station

Keys should change: after a leak, when someone leaves the team, or simply on a schedule. The hard part is the changeover. If the station switches to the new key before the controller does, every command fails, and vice versa.

The usual answer is a key ID (often written kid). Each command says which key signed it, and the station keeps a small keyring. During a changeover it holds both keys; once every controller has switched, you delete the old one:

The kid is not a secret, so it can travel in plain JSON. It does belong inside the signed text in a real design, for the same reason every other field does.

#The whole system on one page

Before planning for failure you need a picture of what can fail. A good system diagram shows each part, what flows between them, and trust boundaries: the lines where data from someone else's control enters yours.

The labels inside each box are its jobs at the boundary. The station validates sensor values and verifies commands; the dashboard validates payloads and judges staleness; only the controller holds the signing key besides the station.

#Decide what happens when each part fails

A failure-mode table lists, for each part: how it fails, how the system notices, and what it does then. Writing it before coding turns "it froze" into a designed behavior.

Part Failure How it's noticed Designed response
Sensor Read raises OSError, or returns an impossible value try/except; range check (DHT22: -40 to 80 °C) Publish an error status; never publish a guessed value
Wi-Fi Connection drops wlan.isconnected() is False, or publish raises OSError Keep sampling into a bounded buffer; reconnect with backoff
Broker Down or unreachable connect() raises Same backoff; flush the buffer, oldest first, once back
Station Power cut or crash Broker publishes the last will Dashboard shows offline; tiles go stale
Fan Station reboots mid-command Boot sequence Fan starts off: Pin(16, Pin.OUT, value=0)
Counter file Corrupted by a power cut during a write int() raises ValueError Refuse commands until it's fixed, rather than restarting at 0
Dashboard Closed, or loses its connection Nothing for the station to notice On reopen, retained status arrives at once

The counter row is a correction to Module 6's load_seq, which returned 0 when the file was unreadable. That is failing open: a corrupted file would quietly re-accept every old command. For anything security-related, prefer failing closed, where the system refuses to act until a person looks.

#Reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter

When the broker goes away, the tempting code is while True: try connect(). It hammers a broker that is already struggling, and it drains a battery. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, up to a cap such as 60 s. After a success, the delay resets to the start.

Backoff alone has a flaw that shows up with many devices. A broker restart disconnects every station at the same moment, so with identical backoff they all retry at the same moments too, in synchronized waves. Jitter fixes that by picking a random delay between 0 and the current ceiling. Here are 30 stations losing a broker that comes back at t = 20 s:

With doubling only, all 30 stations hit the freshly restarted broker within the same instant at t = 31 s, which is how a restart turns into a second outage. With jitter, they trickle in.

The station's connection logic becomes a small state machine. Sampling never stops; only the network part waits:

⚠️ Watch out

Three reconnect bugs. A while not wlan.isconnected() loop with no timeout hangs forever if the network never returns, so give every wait a deadline. A backoff that never resets after success makes the next outage start at a 60-second delay. And a reconnect that forgets to subscribe again leaves the station publishing happily but deaf to commands, because umqtt.simple starts each new connection with no subscriptions.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You committed secrets.py with your broker password last week. Today you add it to .gitignore and commit. Is the password safe?

  • .gitignore only affects files git isn't already tracking, and it never touches history.

  • That stops tracking the file from now on, but last week's commit still contains the password.

  • Rotation makes the leaked value worthless. Cleaning the history is optional, rotation isn't.

Show answer

C. Rotation makes the leaked value worthless. Cleaning the history is optional, rotation isn't.

2A station's key leaked. It shares one key with nine other stations. What does per-device keying change?

  • A shared key means one leak unlocks every device that holds it.

  • Key length protects against guessing, not against a key that has been copied.

  • They don't prevent leaks; they limit how much one leak can unlock.

Show answer

A. A shared key means one leak unlocks every device that holds it.

3Fifty stations use exponential backoff without jitter, starting at 1 s and doubling. The broker restarts. What happens?

  • Their delays grow, but identically, so they stay in step with each other.

  • Same start time and same formula give the same retry times. Random jitter breaks the synchrony.

  • A cap limits the delay; it doesn't stop retrying.

Show answer

B. Same start time and same formula give the same retry times. Random jitter breaks the synchrony.

4The counter file is unreadable after a power cut. Which response fails closed?

  • That re-accepts every old command, which is failing open.

  • It might happen to work, but it can also lock out genuine commands unpredictably, and it hides the problem.

  • Security decisions wait for a human, while the harmless parts of the system keep working.

Show answer

C. Security decisions wait for a human, while the harmless parts of the system keep working.

Key takeaways

  • Secrets leak from code, git history, public projects, screenshots, logs, and the device itself. Plan for each.
  • Keep secrets in a git-ignored secrets.py, commit a secrets.example.py, and on regular Python avoid the name secrets.
  • A leaked secret is fixed by rotating it, not by deleting it. Key IDs let you rotate without downtime.
  • Draw the system with its trust boundaries, then write a failure-mode table: failure, how it's noticed, designed response.
  • Fail closed for security decisions and fail safe for actuators: no command means the fan stays off.
  • Reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, reset it after success, and resubscribe after every reconnect.

#Further reading

  • About secret scanning (GitHub Docs) (opens in a new tab): how GitHub detects committed tokens, and what it can and can't catch.
  • gitignore documentation (opens in a new tab): pattern rules, and the note that already-tracked files aren't affected.
  • Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library) (opens in a new tab): why big systems add jitter, from people who run very large fleets of servers.

m7-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Move every secret into secrets.py and split the station into small files with one job each.
  • Build and test an outbox that never grows past its limit and never loses a message it hasn't sent.
  • Build a backoff timer with jitter, and see how its cap trades recovery speed against load.
  • Run the Pico W's network as a state machine that never blocks sampling, resubscribes after reconnecting, and fails closed on a damaged counter.
  • Cut the Wi-Fi on purpose with a button and watch the station recover.

Right now, if Wi-Fi drops for a minute, the station from Module 6 crashes on its next publish with an OSError and stays dead until someone presses reset. By the end of this lesson the same outage is a non-event: readings pile up in an outbox, the station retries with growing, randomized waits, and when the network returns it reconnects, resubscribes to its fan topic, and delivers the backlog in order.

Module 4's logger already queued readings through an outage. An MQTT station has more to put back together afterward: a broker connection, a subscription that silently disappears, a retained status, and a fan that must stay in a safe state the whole time.

Here is a run you'll be able to reproduce, with the button pressed once to cut the Wi-Fi (your numbers will differ, because the waits are random):

The project ends up with six files, each with one job:

File Job Shared?
main.py Sampling loop and connection state machine Yes
resilience.py Outbox and Backoff classes Yes
commands.py check_command, plus loading and saving the counter Yes
hmac_lite.py HMAC-SHA256 from Module 6 Yes
umqttsimple.py The MQTT library Yes
secrets.py Wi-Fi details and the fan key Never

#Step 1: Move the secrets out

Create secrets.py in the Wokwi project with every value that grants access, and a secrets.example.py with the same names and fake values for anyone you share the project with:

Wokwi-GUEST has no password, so here the Wi-Fi values are harmless. They live in this file anyway, because the day you move the code to a real Pico W at home, this is the only file that changes, and it's the one file that never leaves your machine. If you save the project on Wokwi, remember that free projects are public: use a throwaway fan key there, and keep real keys only in files on your own computer.

#Step 2: An outbox that is bounded and loses nothing it hasn't sent

During an outage, readings keep coming every five seconds. Storing them all eventually fills the Pico's RAM. The outbox therefore has a capacity, and a policy for when it's full: drop the oldest reading, because a recent reading is worth more than an old one, and count how many were dropped so the dashboard can be told.

The other rule is in flush: a message is removed only after send succeeds. If the link dies in the middle of a flush, the unsent messages stay put.

random.getrandbits is used for jitter because it exists on both MicroPython and regular Python. Here are both classes, followed by a 90-second simulated run with the link down from t = 20 s to t = 60 s and a deliberately small outbox of 6:

Read the result carefully, because it shows both the design working and its price:

  • Nothing crashed, and every reading from before and after the outage arrived, in order.
  • Seq 5 to 9 were dropped, because 11 readings piled up and the outbox holds 6. The gap is visible in delivered, which is exactly what Module 5's seq gap detector is for. On the Pico, a capacity of 120 holds about five minutes.
  • The link came back at t = 60, but the station only noticed at t = 70, because its last wait was 15 seconds. That is the trade-off the cap controls: a lower cap reconnects sooner and hits the broker harder.

#Step 3: Fail closed on a damaged counter

Move Module 6's command code into commands.py, with one change. The old load_seq got one case wrong: it returned 0 for a damaged file, which would quietly re-accept old commands. The new one tells "no file yet" apart from "file exists but is unreadable", and returns None for the second:

Readings keep flowing when the counter is damaged. Only the security-sensitive part stops, and every refused command says why on the audit topic.

#Step 4: Add a "cut the Wi-Fi" button

Testing recovery means causing failures on demand. Add a pushbutton with the + button and wire one side to GP14 and the other to GND. The code reads it with an internal pull-up resistor, so it reads 1 normally and 0 while pressed. Pressing it calls wlan.disconnect(), which is as close to unplugging the router as the simulator gets.

#Step 5: The connection state machine

The old station had one blocking connect at startup. The new one has a state variable and a network_step() function that does a little bit of work and returns at once, so the sampling loop is never stuck waiting. The states match the diagram from the notes: join_wifi, wait_wifi, connect_broker, online, and backoff.

Three details make it robust:

  • Every wait has a deadline: Wi-Fi gets 15 seconds before the station backs off, and client.connect(timeout=5) gives up on an unreachable broker after 5 seconds. (The timeout argument exists in current copies of umqtt.simple; an old copy will reject it.)
  • connect_broker subscribes again every time. umqtt.simple connects with a clean session, so the broker forgets subscriptions when a connection drops.
  • Every reading goes through the outbox, even while online. There is one path for data, so the "online" and "recovering" cases can't behave differently by accident.

Copy resilience.py from Step 2 into the project without the test code below the # ---- test line; the station only needs the two classes.

#Step 6: Break it on purpose

Run the simulation with the HiveMQ web client subscribed to c4t-lab/a7f3c9/#, and try each failure:

  1. Wi-Fi drop. Press the button. The terminal prints Wi-Fi lost, readings keep queuing, and after a short random wait the station reconnects and flushes. In the web client, a short burst of readings arrives at once, with seq values in order.
  2. Repeat drops. Press the button several times quickly. Each failure before a successful reconnect makes the next wait longer; one success resets it.
  3. Commands after recovery. After a reconnect, publish a freshly signed fan command. It works, which proves the resubscribe happened.
  4. Sensor fault. Stop the simulation, delete the wire to the DHT22's SDA pin, and start again. Instead of readings, the health topic reports sensor read failed every five seconds, and the dashboard's temperature tile goes stale on schedule.
  5. Damaged counter. Add a file named fan_seq.txt to the project containing the word oops, and start the simulation. The station prints its warning, readings flow normally, and every fan command is refused with counter unreadable.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does flush call self.items.pop(0) only after send returns?

  • Removing it first would lose exactly the message that was being sent when the link died.

  • Speed is the same either way; the order is about not losing data.

  • Capacity is enforced in add, and flush only ever shrinks the list.

Show answer

A. Removing it first would lose exactly the message that was being sent when the link died.

2When the outbox is full, it drops the oldest reading. When would dropping the newest be better?

  • Usually, but not for every kind of data.

  • A policy is a choice about which data matters. For a live dashboard, keep the newest; for a record of what went wrong, the oldest can be the valuable part.

  • Capacity changes how much you keep, not which end you should sacrifice.

Show answer

B. A policy is a choice about which data matters. For a live dashboard, keep the newest; for a record of what went wrong, the oldest can be the valuable part.

3After a Wi-Fi drop, the station reconnects and readings arrive, but fan commands are ignored. Which line was most likely forgotten?

  • That only affects how long the next outage's waits are.

  • Each new connection starts with no subscriptions, so the broker has nowhere to send your commands.

  • The will is stored in the client object and sent with each connect(), and it doesn't affect receiving commands.

Show answer

B. Each new connection starts with no subscriptions, so the broker has nowhere to send your commands.

Key takeaways

  • Put every secret in one file that never leaves your machine or the board, and share a secrets.example.py instead.
  • An outbox needs a capacity, a drop policy, and a dropped counter, and it removes a message only after it is sent.
  • Backoff with jitter protects the broker; its cap decides how long recovery can lag behind the network coming back.
  • A non-blocking state machine with deadlines keeps sampling running in every state.
  • After every reconnect: publish online, resubscribe, report drops, then flush oldest first.
  • Fail closed on damaged security state, and keep the harmless parts of the system working.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Save the counter crash-safely: write to fan_seq.tmp, then os.rename it over fan_seq.txt, so a power cut leaves either the old file or the new one, never half of each.
  • Show the health topic on the dashboard as a warning banner, including how many readings were dropped.
  • Add ntptime.settime() after the first successful connection and send a real timestamp with each reading, so a logger can place buffered readings at the moment they were measured.
  • Keep a small outbox in flash as well as RAM, so readings taken during an outage survive a reboot too.

#Further reading

  • MicroPython network.WLAN (opens in a new tab): status() values such as STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD and STAT_NO_AP_FOUND, useful for printing why Wi-Fi failed.
  • MicroPython time module (opens in a new tab): why ticks_diff exists and when ticks values wrap around.
  • Exponential backoff and jitter (AWS Architecture Blog) (opens in a new tab): the simulation that showed "full jitter" works so well, with charts.

What you'll learn

  • Spot secrets in code, logs, and history before anyone else does.
  • Predict what git keeps after a secret is committed and then ignored.
  • Choose a backoff cap from measured load and recovery numbers.
  • Protect high-priority messages in a bounded outbox.
  • Write a failure-mode table and review a full IoT design for security and reliability problems.

#Warm-up: which lines leak?

Each line comes from a station's code. Mark it safe, leaks, or avoid.

  1. print("Joining", WIFI_SSID, "with password", WIFI_PASSWORD)
  2. client.publish(AUDIT, json.dumps({"result": "rejected", "reason": "bad signature"}))
  3. client.publish(HEALTH, "crash: " + repr(err) + " key=" + FAN_KEY.decode())
  4. print("Using fan key", FAN_KEY[:6])
  5. print("Online. Queued messages:", len(box.items))
Show solution
  1. Leaks. Serial output gets copied into chat messages, screenshots, and bug reports.
  2. Safe. A reason and nothing else.
  3. Leaks, and to a public broker, the worst audience there is.
  4. Avoid. Six characters don't hand over the key, but they do make it a little easier to guess, and the habit spreads. Print a key ID like k2 instead.
  5. Safe.

#Exercise 1: A tiny secret scanner

Write scan(files) that takes a dict of file names to contents and reports three kinds of problem: a name containing PASSWORD, KEY, TOKEN, or SECRET assigned a non-empty literal (placeholders such as replace-me don't count), any hex string 32 characters or longer, and a print that mentions KEY or PASSWORD.

Need a hint?

Two regular expressions do most of the work: (\w*(PASSWORD|KEY|TOKEN|SECRET)\w*)\s*=\s*b?["']([^"']+)["'] for assignments (the b? allows b"..." bytes literals) and \b[0-9a-f]{32,}\b for hex. [^"']+ needs at least one character, so WIFI_PASSWORD = "" doesn't match.

Show solution

The note in notes.txt is the sneaky one: no code at all, just a key pasted while testing. Real scanners such as GitHub's work the same way in principle, with hundreds of patterns for known token formats. None can catch everything, which is why secrets belong in a file git never sees.

#Exercise 2: What does git actually keep?

A student runs these commands in a folder containing main.py and secrets.py:

Answer three questions: Is secrets.py still tracked? Is the password in the history? What exactly should the student do now?

Need a hint?

.gitignore only stops untracked files from being added. Think about which commit already contains secrets.py, and whether anything since then removed it.

Show solution

Yes, it is still tracked: the first commit added it, and git keeps tracking files it already knows about. Any later edit to secrets.py will show up in git status and can be committed. And yes, the password is in the history, in the first commit, readable with git show HEAD~1:secrets.py.

The fix, in order:

The .gitignore entry is already in place, so the file won't come back. Rewriting history to remove the first commit's copy is optional cleanup; step 1 is the part that makes the leak harmless.

#Exercise 3: Pick a backoff cap with numbers, not vibes

A longer cap means fewer reconnect attempts during an outage (less load) but a longer wait after the network comes back (more lag). Simulate 2,000 two-minute outages for caps of 4, 16, and 60 seconds, using full jitter from a 1-second base. Report the average number of attempts during the outage and the average and worst lag.

Need a hint?

For one outage: keep a clock t and a failure count n. Each round, add uniform(0, min(cap, 2 ** n)) to t. While t is still inside the outage, that try failed: count it. The first try after the outage ends succeeds, and t - outage is the lag.

Show solution

For one greenhouse station, 61 attempts in two minutes is nothing, and a cap of 4 s gives the fastest recovery. For 500 stations sharing one broker, that becomes 30,000 connection attempts against a broker that is already in trouble, and a cap of 30 to 60 s is kinder. The right cap depends on how many devices share the broker, which is why it's a setting and not a constant buried in the code.

#Exercise 4: Never drop the frost alarm

The outbox from Lesson 2 drops the oldest message when it's full. That's fine for readings, and terrible for a one-off FROST alarm that got queued during an outage. Write PriorityOutbox(capacity) where add(topic, payload, keep=False) marks precious messages. When full, drop the oldest message that isn't marked keep; only if every message is precious, drop the oldest one and count it separately.

Need a hint?

A for ... else loop is handy: search for the first item whose keep flag is False and delete it with break. The else branch runs only when the loop finished without a break, which means everything was precious.

Show solution

FROST survived four readings churning through the box. The second line shows the limit: a flood of alarms eventually pushes out the first one, and alarms lost: 1 makes sure that loss is reported instead of silent. Messages still leave oldest first, so the alarm goes out before the readings that came after it.

#Exercise 5: A failure-mode table for a freezer monitor

A school cafeteria wants a Pico W in its walk-in freezer: a temperature probe, a buzzer, and MQTT alerts to the kitchen manager's dashboard when the freezer rises above -15 °C. Write a failure-mode table with at least six rows: part, failure, how it's noticed, and designed response.

Need a hint?

Go part by part: probe, Pico, power, Wi-Fi (a metal freezer box is a famously bad place for radio), broker, dashboard, and the buzzer itself. For each response, ask: does this fail safe, meaning that it errs toward the manager finding out?

Show solution
Part Failure How it's noticed Designed response
Probe Unplugged or broken Read error or impossible value Sound the buzzer and send a sensor failed alert; a broken probe must never look like "all fine"
Probe Stuck at one value Value unchanged for 30 minutes (a real freezer always wobbles a little) Send a sensor suspicious warning
Wi-Fi No signal from inside the freezer Connect times out Mount the Pico outside the door with only the probe cable inside; the buzzer works with no network at all
Power Outage or unplugged Broker publishes the last will offline Dashboard shows a red offline banner; a freezer monitor that's off is itself an alarm
Broker Down Station's connect fails Back off and queue alerts with keep=True; the buzzer still sounds locally
Dashboard Nobody looking Alert not acknowledged within 10 minutes Repeat the alert every 10 minutes until someone acknowledges it
Buzzer Broken Can't detect without extra hardware Test it weekly with a "buzzer test" button and log each test

The thread through every row: silence must never mean "fine." Each failure either makes noise locally, shows up as offline or stale remotely, or both.

#Exercise 6: Review a design

A team presents this classroom CO2 monitor. Find at least six problems, and give a fix for each.

  • The Pico W publishes to co2 on broker.hivemq.com, with the value as a bare number.
  • A teacher's phone app opens a window motor by publishing open to co2/window.
  • main.py contains WIFI_PASSWORD = "Room214!" and lives in a public GitHub repository.
  • The dashboard shows each value with element.innerHTML = payload.
  • If the sensor fails, the code publishes the last good value so the chart has no gaps.
  • When the broker is unreachable, the code retries connect() in a tight loop.
Need a hint?

Sort your findings into the three halves of this course: messages a dashboard can understand (Module 5), commands only the right person can send (Module 6), and secrets and failures (Module 7). Each bullet has at least one problem.

Show solution
  1. Ambiguous topic and payload. Use c4t-lab/<code>/school/room214/co2 with {"v": 812, "unit": "ppm", "dev": "...", "seq": ...}, and a retained status with a last will.
  2. Anyone can open the window. Sign commands with HMAC and a counter, or use a private broker with an ACL so only the teacher's account can write to the window topic. Ideally both.
  3. A school Wi-Fi password in a public repo. Change the password now, move it to a git-ignored secrets.py, and run git rm --cached on any tracked copy.
  4. innerHTML with broker data lets a stranger run script in the dashboard. Validate the payload and display it with textContent.
  5. Publishing stale values as fresh hides the failure. Publish a sensor failed health message and let the dashboard mark the tile stale; a gap in the chart is the truth.
  6. The tight retry loop hammers the broker and starves the rest of the program. Use exponential backoff with jitter, and keep the main loop non-blocking.

Bonus: a public broker is wrong for a real classroom anyway. Data about a specific room in a specific school is exactly what HiveMQ and Mosquitto ask you not to publish.

#Challenge: Test a reconnect state machine without hardware

Model the station's connection logic in plain Python, with a fake clock that ticks once per second. step(now, wifi_up, broker_up) moves through join_wifi, wait_wifi (5-second deadline), connect_broker, online, and backoff (full jitter, 1-second base, 16-second cap). One step may pass through several states. Run a scenario with Wi-Fi down from 10 to 30 s and the broker down from 50 to 70 s, and check three properties: it subscribes on every connect, it's back online within 21 s of each outage ending, and the backoff has reset by the end.

Need a hint?

Write step() as a chain of separate if statements rather than if/elif, in the same order as the arrows, so a station whose retry time arrives while Wi-Fi is already up can go from backoff all the way to online in one tick. Put the subscribe count and the backoff reset in the one place the station becomes online, and neither can be forgotten.

Show solution

The broker outage shows backoff growing (1, 1, 3, 2, 10, 10 s) while the Wi-Fi is fine, and the station returned at t = 77, seven seconds after the broker did: well inside the 21-second budget of a 16-second cap plus the 5-second Wi-Fi deadline. Testing the state machine this way takes a second; testing it by unplugging a router takes an afternoon.

What you'll learn

  • Choose a capstone project that fits your level and still meets every requirement.
  • Write a topic plan, payload schema, and command list that a dashboard and a station can both rely on.
  • Draw the system with its trust boundaries and list the threats at each boundary.
  • Write a failure-mode table and a secrets inventory before writing device code.
  • Check the plan with a script that catches common design mistakes.

A greenhouse that texts you when it's too hot is easy to sketch on a napkin. The napkin version leaves out who else can switch the fan, what the dashboard shows when the station dies, and where the Wi-Fi password lives. Those parts take longer than the sensors, and they are what this capstone is graded on.

You'll build a complete monitoring system in Wokwi (or on a real Pico W, if you have one): sensors, a station that publishes over MQTT, a dashboard, at least one remote action that only you can trigger, and documentation that lets someone else understand and test it. This lesson is the plan. The next one builds it in milestones, and the last one tests, polishes, and grades it.

#The brief

Your system must have all eight of these. The project ideas below differ in how hard each one is, not in which ones they skip.

# Requirement Where you learned it
1 At least two sensor readings, validated against realistic ranges Modules 3 and 7
2 Readings collected on a non-blocking schedule, with sequence numbers Modules 4 and 5
3 MQTT with a written topic plan, JSON payloads with units, and a retained status with a last will Module 5
4 A dashboard that shows fresh, stale, and offline states clearly Module 5
5 At least one remote action protected by HMAC signatures and replay protection, with an audit topic Module 6
6 Every secret in a git-ignored secrets.py, with a secrets.example.py Module 7
7 Designed failure behavior: outbox, backoff with jitter, resubscribe, safe defaults, fail-closed security state Module 7
8 A README with an architecture diagram, topic plan, threat table, failure table, and test results This module

#Pick a project

Project Level Wokwi parts Remote action What makes it interesting
Plant-care monitor Starter Potentiometer standing in for a soil-moisture probe, photoresistor Signed water_now; an LED is the pump The pump must switch itself off after 10 s even if the "off" command never arrives
Smart greenhouse Core DHT22, photoresistor, LED fan, servo vent Signed fan on/off and vent angle Commands with an argument (the angle), range-checked after the signature
Weather station Core DHT22, photoresistor, pushbutton as a rain-gauge bucket Signed set_interval A configuration command that changes how the station behaves, plus counting events
Freezer monitor Stretch DS18B20 temperature sensor, buzzer Signed ack_alarm A local alarm that works with no network, and alerts that repeat until someone acknowledges them
Two-site monitor Stretch Two Pico W stations in two Wokwi tabs Signed commands with a different key per station Per-device keys, key IDs, and rotating one station's key while the other keeps working

If you're unsure, pick a core project and do it well. A complete starter project with excellent tests beats a stretch project with three requirements half-done.

#Fill in the plan

Copy this template into a file called PLAN.md in your project and fill in every section. Short answers are fine; blank ones aren't.

Here is the architecture for the weather station, as an example of the level of detail to aim for:

#Find the threats at each boundary

Threat modeling sounds grand, but for a project this size it is one question asked four times. For every arrow that crosses a trust boundary, ask whether someone could read it, fake it, replay it, or block it, and what stops them. For the weather station:

Arrow Read? Faked? Replayed? Blocked? Defense
Readings to broker Yes, public broker Yes, anyone can publish to the topic Yes Yes, a Wi-Fi outage Nothing secret in them; the dashboard validates and checks seq; outbox through outages
set_interval to station Yes Only with the key Yes, without a counter Yes HMAC over device|command|argument|seq; counter saved to flash; range check 5 to 300 s
Status to dashboard Yes Yes Yes Yes Accepted as a hint only; staleness is judged by the dashboard's own clock
Key on the station Anyone holding the board can copy it No No No One key per station; a rotation plan in the secrets inventory

The third row is an honest one. On a public broker, a stranger can publish a fake online, and the dashboard can't tell. Writing that down, along with "a private broker with ACLs would fix this," is better than pretending the problem doesn't exist.

#Check the plan with a script

Some design mistakes are mechanical enough to catch automatically. Write your plan as a Python dictionary and run it through this checker. The example has three deliberate mistakes:

The rain gauge is the instructive one: "no unit" for a count of bucket tips sounds pedantic until the dashboard has to decide whether 3 means millimetres, tips, or tips per hour. Replace the example with your own plan and run it until it prints 0 problem(s) found.

💡 Tip

Add checks of your own as you go. If your project has commands with arguments, check that every argument has a range. If it has two stations, check that no two devices share a key ID.

#Milestones

The next lesson builds the project in six milestones. Each ends with something you can see working, so you always have a version to fall back on.

Milestone Done when
M1: Sensors Every reading prints with a unit, and out-of-range values are caught
M2: Publishing Readings, retained status, and last will appear correctly in the HiveMQ web client
M3: Dashboard Tiles show fresh, stale, and offline, and junk payloads are ignored
M4: Remote action Genuine commands work; replays, forgeries, and out-of-range arguments are refused and audited
M5: Resilience A Wi-Fi cut, a broker outage, and a reboot all recover without losing control or the counter
M6: Documentation README complete; someone else can follow it to run and test the system

Before moving on, check your plan against the eight requirements one more time. A missing requirement is cheap to add to a plan and expensive to add to finished code.

What you'll learn

  • Organize the project so settings, secrets, logic, hardware, and the main loop each live in their own file.
  • Generalize signed commands to carry a range-checked argument.
  • Test the station's decision logic on your computer before it runs on the Pico.
  • Build and verify each milestone before starting the next, keeping a working version at every step.

The examples here use the weather station from the planning lesson, with a DHT22, a photoresistor, a pushbutton as a rain gauge, and a signed set_interval command. If you picked another project, the structure stays the same; only sensors.py, RANGES, COMMANDS, and apply_command change.

#The project layout

File What's in it Changes per project?
config.py Topic names, device name, intervals: settings that are safe to share Yes
secrets.py / secrets.example.py Wi-Fi details and keys / the same names with fake values Yes
logic.py validate_reading, check_command: pure Python, tested on your computer Only RANGES and COMMANDS
sensors.py Reads the hardware and returns (where, what, value, unit) tuples Yes
resilience.py, hmac_lite.py, umqttsimple.py Outbox and backoff, HMAC, MQTT No
main.py Loop and connection state machine from Module 7 A little
dashboard.html, sign_command.py, README.md The computer side and the documentation Yes

Settings and secrets are split on purpose. config.py can go in a screenshot or a public repository; secrets.py never does.

#The starter logic, with commands that take an argument

Module 6's commands were just names. Real projects need values: an interval, an angle, a duration. The argument goes inside the signed text (device|command|argument|seq, with an empty argument for commands that take none), and after the signature is verified, the station checks it against an allowed range. A signed set_interval 1 is still refused, because one second would flood the broker.

On your computer, the standard library stands in for hmac_lite.py, so this cell runs here unchanged:

On the Pico, logic.py starts with import json and from hmac_lite import hmac_sha256_hex, same instead of the stand-ins above the dashed line.

Now the tests. They are the part of the starter worth the most: every time you change logic.py, run them again. Add a test for each rule your own project adds.

The test names read like the requirements, which is deliberate: in the last lesson this output becomes evidence in your README.

#M1: Sensors that report honestly

Wire your parts and write sensors.py. Its only job is to read hardware and return tuples; it doesn't know about MQTT. Here is the weather station's version, including a rain gauge that counts button presses with an interrupt:

Done when: a loop that calls read_all() and validate_reading() every few seconds prints every value with its unit; dragging the DHT22's sliders changes the numbers; and pressing the button raises rain. Check which way your light value moves when you cover the photoresistor, and write it in your plan.

#M2: Publishing that matches the plan

Start from Module 7's main.py. Import config, logic, and sensors, and replace its sample() with one that validates every reading and reports problems on the health topic instead of publishing them:

In the main loop, use every_ms instead of the fixed EVERY_MS when you schedule the next sample, so M4's command can change it.

Done when: the HiveMQ web client, subscribed to your prefix with #, shows every topic from your plan with the right payloads, the retained status arrives first, and stopping the simulation produces offline within about 45 seconds.

#M3: A dashboard that tells the truth

Reuse the dashboard from Module 5 with three changes:

  1. Add your units to UNITS, or the dashboard will rightly ignore your readings: for the weather station, tips: "tips".
  2. Show the health topic. A simple version: in show(), if parts[2] === "health", write the error text into a banner element with textContent.
  3. Make offline impossible to miss. When a status badge says offline, add the stale class to every tile from that device.

Done when: tiles go stale after three missed intervals; stopping the simulation shows offline; disconnecting the DHT22's data wire shows a health banner; and publishing {"v": "<b>hi</b>", "unit": "C"} to a reading topic changes nothing on screen.

#M4: A remote action only you can trigger

Point the station's subscription at config.COMMAND_TOPIC, and route accepted commands through one function that holds every project-specific effect:

The signing tool learns about arguments too:

Done when: a genuine command takes effect and is audited as accepted, and each of these is refused with the right reason: the same message again, the argument edited, a signed but out-of-range argument, a command for another device, and plain text. The last lesson gives you a script that generates all of these at once.

⚠️ Watch out

If your project has an actuator (a pump, a fan, a heater), it needs a safe default that doesn't depend on any command arriving: off at boot (Pin(..., value=0)), and for anything that runs, a timer that switches it off by itself. "The off command got lost" must never mean "the pump runs all night."

#M5: Survive outages and reboots

Module 7's state machine, outbox, and backoff carry over as they are. What's new is testing them against your project:

  • Cut Wi-Fi with the button for 10 seconds, then for 2 minutes. Readings from the short outage all arrive; the long one reports a dropped count on the health topic if the outbox filled.
  • Send a command, cut the Wi-Fi, restore it, and send another command with the next seq. It must work, proving the resubscribe.
  • Restart the simulation and replay your last command. On a real Pico it is refused; in Wokwi the counter file resets, so write down in your README what you'd do about it (Module 6's practice lesson has one answer).

Done when: every failure row in your plan's failure table has been triggered at least once, and the response matched the table, or you've updated the table to match what you decided is right.

#M6: Documentation someone else can use

A project nobody else can run is only half finished. Your README.md should let a classmate open your Wokwi project, run it, and attack it without asking you anything.

Write the "What is NOT protected" section honestly. "On the public broker anyone can publish a fake online status" is a strength in a README, because it shows you understand your own system.

Done when: a classmate follows the README from a fresh copy of your project to a working dashboard and a refused replay, and you didn't have to explain anything out loud.

What you'll learn

  • Write a test plan with normal, boundary, failure, and security tests, and record real results.
  • Generate a complete set of attack messages for your station and confirm each is refused for the right reason.
  • Polish code and documentation so a stranger can run and test the project.
  • Present the system in four minutes, including a live failure and a live attack.
  • Assess your own work against the rubric, and choose what to learn next.

A demo that only shows the system working proves the least interesting thing about it. Anyone's station publishes a temperature when nothing goes wrong. Yours should also be shown going offline and coming back, refusing a replayed command, and marking a dead sensor as dead, because those are the behaviors you designed, and the ones a user would never see otherwise.

#Write a test plan with four kinds of test

Kind What it checks Weather-station example
Unit One function's logic, on your computer test_logic.py from the previous lesson: ten tests, all passing
Normal use The whole system doing its job Readings for every topic in the plan appear every 10 s with correct units
Boundary Values at the edges of what's allowed DHT22 slider at -40 °C and 80 °C is accepted; set_interval 5 and 300 accepted, 4 and 301 refused
Failure Each row of your failure table Wi-Fi cut for 2 minutes: no crash, readings resume in order, dropped reported
Security Each row of your threat table Every message from the attack kit below is refused with the expected reason

Record each test as a row you can paste into your README:

The Actual column is the important one. "It worked" is not a result; numbers and quoted output are.

#Generate the attack kit for your station

Typing ten hand-edited attack messages into the web client is slow and error-prone. This script makes them from your key, your device name, and the last seq your station accepted, and says what the audit topic should report for each. Change the three settings at the top, run it on your computer, and publish each message in order to your command topic:

S3 and S4 are the same attack aimed at different fields: they show that the argument and the counter are both covered by the signature. S5 to S7 are signed with the real key, so they test the checks that protect you from your own mistakes. If any result differs from the expectation, you've found a real bug, which is the best possible outcome of a test. Fix it, add a unit test for it, and record both.

#Polish it for a stranger

Go through this list with your project open. Each item is something graders and classmates notice in the first two minutes.

  • secrets.py is not in the repository or the shared Wokwi project; secrets.example.py is, with fake values.
  • No print or MQTT message anywhere contains a key or password. Search your files for KEY and PASSWORD.
  • Every topic in the code matches the README's topic table exactly.
  • config.py holds every setting a user might change; nothing is buried in main.py.
  • Comments explain why ("fail closed: a damaged counter must not reset to 0"), not what ("set x to 0").
  • Debugging leftovers are gone: commented-out experiments, unused functions, print("here").
  • Actuators start in their safe state, and anything that runs has an automatic off.
  • A fresh copy of the project, set up only by following the README, works on the first try.

The last item is the one people skip and the one that fails most often. Ask a classmate to do it while you watch without helping.

#Present it in four minutes

A good technical demo is a story with evidence. This order works because each part sets up the next:

  1. Problem. Who would use this and what goes wrong without it. One sentence, one picture.
  2. Architecture. Your diagram, pointing at the trust boundaries.
  3. Normal use. Dashboard live; drag a sensor slider; the tile updates.
  4. Failure. Press the Wi-Fi cut button or stop the simulation. Point at offline and the stale tiles, then show the recovery and the backlog arriving in order.
  5. Attack. Publish a genuine command (it works), then publish it again (refused, and the audit topic says why).
  6. Limits and next. Read your "What is NOT protected" section aloud. It shows you know where the edges of your design are.

Rehearse it twice with a timer. Prepare the signed commands in advance with the right seq values, and keep a short screen recording of a successful run in case the Wokwi gateway is slow on the day.

#Rubric

Score each row from 1 to 4. A 3 in every row is a strong project; a 4 means you went beyond what the brief asked for.

Criterion 1: Beginning 2: Developing 3: Proficient 4: Exemplary
Sensors and data quality Readings print, no validation Some range checks; failures crash or publish fake values Every reading validated; failures reported on a health topic Also detects stuck or implausible sensors; calibration documented
MQTT design Topics ad hoc, bare numbers Topic plan exists but code drifts from it; units missing in places Code matches the plan; JSON with units, device, and seq; retained status with last will Plan checked by script; QoS and retain choices justified in the README
Dashboard Shows numbers Shows latest values; staleness unclear Fresh, stale, and offline states clear; junk payloads ignored; textContent only Health banner, gap detection from seq, or history charts
Remote action and authentication Unsigned commands Signed, but replays or edited fields get through HMAC over every field, counter replay protection, allowlist and range checks, audit topic Per-device keys, key IDs, or a counter that survives Wokwi restarts
Credentials Secrets in main.py Separate file, but leaked in a log, repo, or shared project secrets.py ignored, secrets.example.py shared, nothing secret printed or published Rotation plan written and demonstrated
Failure handling Crashes on the first outage Recovers from some failures, or blocks while recovering Outbox, backoff with jitter, resubscribe, safe defaults, fail-closed counter Every failure-table row tested with recorded results
Testing evidence None A few manual checks, no records Unit tests pass; attack kit run with results recorded; failure tests recorded Found and fixed a real bug through testing, with a test added for it
Documentation and presentation README missing or a few lines README exists; a stranger needs help A stranger can run and test it from the README; demo shows normal use, a failure, and an attack Honest limits section; clear diagrams; demo within time and rehearsed

#Reflect

Write short answers to these in your README, under a heading called Reflection:

  1. Which failure surprised you most when you triggered it, and what did you change because of it?
  2. Where does your system still trust something it shouldn't? What would it take to fix that?
  3. If 100 copies of your station shared one broker, what would break first?
  4. What would you do differently if you started again tomorrow?

#Where to go next

  • Run your own broker. Install Mosquitto on a Raspberry Pi or your laptop, turn on allow_anonymous false with a password file and an ACL file, then add TLS with a certificate. Everything you signed by hand becomes a second layer of defense instead of the only one.
  • Give each device its own certificate. Mutual TLS, where the broker also checks the device's certificate, is how large IoT platforms identify millions of devices.
  • Store and chart history. Send readings into a time-series database such as InfluxDB and chart them with Grafana, or build flows and dashboards in Node-RED.
  • Build it for real. A physical Pico W adds problems the simulator hides: power supplies, weatherproofing, Wi-Fi range, and sensors that drift.
  • Learn MQTT 5. It adds features such as message expiry, which is a cleaner answer to "is this retained reading too old?" than anything in MQTT 3.1.1.

#Further reading

  • Mosquitto documentation (opens in a new tab): configuration, authentication, and ACL guides for running your own broker.
  • Node-RED: create your first flow (opens in a new tab): the quickest route to a flow-based dashboard that subscribes to MQTT.
  • OWASP Internet of Things Project (opens in a new tab): check your finished system against the IoT Top 10 and see how many you've already handled.
